The deployment of machine learning techniques within our Adaptive Learning Systems emphasizes the significant enhancements achievable in personalized curriculum design. The results, as illustrated in Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Fig. 4 ‣ V-F Integration of Machine Learning for Curriculum Design ‣ V Experiments ‣ Adaptive Learning Systems: Personalized Curriculum Design Using LLM-Powered Analytics"), highlight the effectiveness of various models and their corresponding techniques in adapting educational content.

Dynamic adjustment and real-time analysis generate measurable improvements. The Llama-3-7b model, utilizing dynamic adjustment strategies, achieved a notable improvement of 15.4% in learner engagement. Furthermore, GPT-4, which employed real-time analysis, outperformed this by attaining an 18.7% improvement. These improvements underscore the potential of adaptive systems to enhance the educational experience significantly.

Adaptability and user satisfaction are crucial metrics. In terms of adaptability level, the Llama-3-7b model displays a high adaptability rating, while GPT-4 exemplifies a very high level of adaptability. User satisfaction metrics further reflect successful implementation, with 85% of users satisfied with the Llama-3-7b model and an increased satisfaction rate of 90% with the responses generated by GPT-4. The strong performance in both adaptability and user satisfaction indicates the framework’s substantial contribution to enriching instructional methods.

Consequently, the integration of LLM-powered analytics into curriculum design demonstrates a progressive shift that enhances student engagement, tailoring educational experiences and responding effectively to learners’ needs.

## VI Conclusions

We present a framework for Adaptive Learning Systems that employs LLM-powered analytics for personalized curriculum design. This innovative method customizes educational content to meet the specific needs of each student, leveraging real-time data analysis to inform teaching strategies. By implementing advanced machine learning techniques, our framework dynamically modifies learning pathways and recommends resources that reflect learners’ progress, preferences, and performance metrics. Continuous assessment allows for instructional strategies to adapt, providing learners with engaging and relevant material tailored to their individual requirements. Our experimental results indicate marked enhancements in learner engagement and knowledge retention, emphasizing the advantages of a customized curriculum. Comprehensive evaluations conducted across various educational contexts further affirm the system’s flexibility and positive impact on learning outcomes. This framework aspires to revolutionize traditional educational practices, leading to a more responsive and effective learning experience for all students.

args.summary:
This paper presents a framework for Adaptive Learning Systems that leverages LLM-powered analytics (specifically Llama-3-7b and GPT-4) for personalized curriculum design. The system uses real-time data analysis to dynamically adjust learning pathways and recommend resources based on individual student progress, preferences, and performance metrics. Key methodological components include personalized curriculum formulation through feedback loops, dynamic learning pathways with reinforcement mechanisms, and real-time data analysis for continuous adaptation.

**Experimental Results:**
- GPT-4 consistently outperformed Llama-3-7b across all metrics, achieving LES scores of 80.5-84.3% and KRR of 82.7-87.5% across five datasets.
- The real-time feedback mechanism yielded the highest engagement increase (19.2%) and retention improvement (22.4%).
- Adaptive sequencing achieved a 22.1% engagement increase and 23.4% retention improvement.
- Ablation studies confirmed that removing real-time adjustment, personalized recommendations, or dynamic pathways significantly reduced performance.
- User satisfaction reached 85% for Llama-3-7b and 90% for GPT-4.

The framework was evaluated across diverse educational contexts using datasets including Low-Resource Language, MCScript, Families in Wild, ETHICS, and Simulated Annotated data, with 10,000 student interactions over 20 epochs and batch size of 16.

# Dynamic Strategy Adaptation in Multi-Agent Environments with Large Language Models

###### Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong reasoning abilities across mathematical, strategic, and linguistic tasks, yet little is known about how well they reason in dynamic, real-time, multi-agent scenarios, such as collaborative environments in which agents continuously adapt to each other’s behavior, as in cooperative gameplay settings. In this paper, we bridge this gap by combining LLM-driven agents with strategic reasoning and real-time adaptation in cooperative, multi-agent environments grounded in game-theoretic principles such as belief consistency and Nash equilibrium. The proposed framework applies broadly to dynamic scenarios in which agents coordinate, communicate, and make decisions in response to continuously changing conditions. We provide real-time strategy refinement and adaptive feedback mechanisms that enable agents to dynamically adjust policies based on immediate contextual interactions, in contrast to previous efforts that evaluate LLM capabilities in static or turn-based settings. Empirical results show that our method achieves up to a 26% improvement in return over PPO baselines in high-noise environments, while maintaining real-time latency under 1.05 milliseconds. Our approach improves collaboration efficiency, task completion rates, and flexibility, illustrating that game-theoretic guidance integrated with real-time feedback enhances LLM performance, ultimately fostering more resilient and flexible strategic multi-agent systems.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are an effective machine learning tool that can perform a broad range of reasoning tasks, such as mathematical problem solving, code generation, commonsense inference, and strategic board games. However, their ability to operate effectively in real-time, multi-agent coordination settings remains under-explored [[1](#bib.bib1)]. Given the rise of multi-agent systems, characterized by dynamic collaboration and automation, there is a need for new frameworks capable of supporting real-time strategic adaptation. Although game theory offers a robust mathematical framework for modeling strategic interactions, it typically assumes fixed decision rules that lack the flexibility to accommodate real-world complexity and change [[1](#bib.bib1)]. In contrast, reinforcement learning (RL) provides a flexible mechanism for learning through experience; however, it requires extensive training and often produces strategies that lack clear interpretability. To guide this investigation, we ask the following research question: How can LLMs dynamically adapt and refine their game strategies based on real-time feedback in multi-agent, multi-turn environments to achieve enhanced rationality and equilibrium outcomes?

A number of prior works have [[2](#bib.bib2), [3](#bib.bib3), [4](#bib.bib4), [5](#bib.bib5), [6](#bib.bib6), [7](#bib.bib7), [8](#bib.bib8), [9](#bib.bib9), [10](#bib.bib10), [11](#bib.bib11), [12](#bib.bib12), [13](#bib.bib13)] studied negotiation, tool integration, real-time planning, and embodied reasoning in the context of LLM-based decision-making. For example, He et al. [[2](#bib.bib2)] and Lewis et al. [[3](#bib.bib3)] explore end-to-end learning for negotiation dialogues, while Toolformer [[4](#bib.bib4)] demonstrates how LLMs can autonomously learn to invoke external tools during generation. PaLM-E [[5](#bib.bib5)] highlights the value of integrating visual and proprioceptive inputs for grounded multimodal reasoning. ReAct prompting [[6](#bib.bib6)] illustrates how models can reason and act by interleaving tool calls with intermediate steps. NegotiationArena [[7](#bib.bib7)] and StarCraft II benchmarks [[8](#bib.bib8)] provide multi-agent coordination evaluations, and CICERO [[9](#bib.bib9)] showcases strategic interaction through dialogue in high-stakes, turn-based environments. Recent frameworks such as CAMEL [[10](#bib.bib10)], AutoGen [[11](#bib.bib11)], LangAgent [[12](#bib.bib12)], and Voyager [[13](#bib.bib13)] have introduced collaborative LLM teams with structured roles and planning objectives.

Other solutions such as SWE-agent [[14](#bib.bib14)] and MetaGPT [[15](#bib.bib15)] propose programming-based role assignment and skill composition pipelines, yet often operate with fixed dialogue states and precomputed coordination graphs. OctoAgents [[16](#bib.bib16)] explore zero-shot LLM team formation but require architectural homogeneity and lack continual learning mechanisms. The MindAct [[17](#bib.bib17)] and CoLLM [[18](#bib.bib18)] models examine collaboration over temporal chains but still assume a known world model. While prior solutions [[2](#bib.bib2), [3](#bib.bib3), [4](#bib.bib4), [5](#bib.bib5), [6](#bib.bib6), [7](#bib.bib7), [8](#bib.bib8), [9](#bib.bib9), [10](#bib.bib10), [11](#bib.bib11), [12](#bib.bib12), [13](#bib.bib13)] enable symbolic reasoning, tool usage, and basic interagent dialogue, they typically do not support continuous strategic adaptation in cooperative, real-time environments. Most of these existing approaches operate in static settings or rely on single-shot policy inference. There is little ability for agents to revise goals, respond to degraded teammate performance, or restructure plans in response to unforeseen environment transitions. A central open challenge is, thus, how to enable agents to adjust their strategy mid-execution using context-aware feedback, memory persistence, symbolic priors, and feedback-aware control loops that reflect real-time game-theoretic dynamics.

An examination of the literature that addresses uncertainty, partial observability, and strategic adaptation in games reveals several key limitations [[19](#bib.bib19), [20](#bib.bib20), [21](#bib.bib21), [13](#bib.bib13), [22](#bib.bib22), [23](#bib.bib23), [24](#bib.bib24), [9](#bib.bib9), [25](#bib.bib25)]. GTBench [[19](#bib.bib19)] tests LLMs on game-theoretic matrix tasks, finding poor robustness in partially observable environments. GameTheoryLLM [[20](#bib.bib20)] formalizes Bayesian agent workflows for negotiation but imposes synchronous update protocols. RationalLLM [[21](#bib.bib21)] studies equilibrium behavior but does not support belief evolution or policy trajectory tracking. MARL benchmarks like MAgent [[26](#bib.bib26)] and EnvAgent [[27](#bib.bib27)] test emergent roles but fail to align agents with structured symbolic constraints. Systems like MindAgent [[28](#bib.bib28)], DEAM [[29](#bib.bib29)], and ToM-GPT [[30](#bib.bib30)] simulate theory-of-mind and belief graphs but rely on heavily curated scenarios. CoaLLM [[31](#bib.bib31)] and OpenAgents [[32](#bib.bib32)] attempt to unify self-play and LLM planning, though they still assume pre-scripted task flows.

Although CICERO [[9](#bib.bib9)] offers a rich symbolic policy in the context of Diplomacy, it is limited to turn-based play. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) [[25](#bib.bib25)] allows reward shaping but lacks dynamic revision based on environment evolution. Existing frameworks such as like RolePlay [[33](#bib.bib33)] and ThoughtAgents [[34](#bib.bib34)] aim to inject personality and dialogue abstraction but do not connect memory or belief state with performance feedback. Few systems track and utilize contextual priors across time steps. Even fewer are capable of aligning their behavioral revisions with task-level metrics like regret, coordination efficiency, or Nash deviation. We argue that bridging this gap requires dynamic feedback systems that are tightly coupled with symbolic modeling and game-theoretic planning principles. The field still lacks a unified method for enabling LLM-based agents to revise their strategies in real-time as goals shift, agents deviate, or coordination structures deteriorate.

The strategic use of LLMs in dynamic, real-time, multi-agent environments faces a significant open problem: how to enable agents to reason adaptively, coordinate under uncertainty, and revise decisions as environments evolve. While early systems [[19](#bib.bib19), [20](#bib.bib20), [21](#bib.bib21), [13](#bib.bib13), [22](#bib.bib22), [23](#bib.bib23), [9](#bib.bib9)] have made progress in specific areas, such as static equilibrium modeling, symbolic dialogue protocols, or role-based planning, they remain limited in three key aspects: 1) they are unable to revise beliefs in response to shifting goals or noisy conditions, 2) they lack real-time mechanisms for coordination across agents, and 3) they do not incorporate symbolic priors or game-theoretic principles into feedback loops. These limitations highlight the need for integrated multi-agent reasoning frameworks that support real-time strategy adaptation and structured coordination, guided by symbolic feedback and contextual understanding under uncertainty.

The main contribution of this paper is to address the limitations of static decision-making methods, including rule-based strategies, turn-based reasoning, and offline reinforcement learning, by proposing a new framework that enables agents to adapt strategies in real time using LLM-guided reward shaping. By integrating symbolic evaluations from a frozen language model with a reinforcement learning loop, the proposed system refines agent behavior based on contextual signals such as order progress and timestep. This hybrid framework is designed to support collaboration in unpredictable, noisy environments where conventional policies tend to fail. In addition to developing the architecture, the proposed framework is empirically evaluated across dynamic environments to assess performance, robustness to noise, and latency tradeoffs. The proposed method delivers strategic benefits while preserving real-time inference speeds. In summary, the key contributions of this paper are:

We assess the performance of our framework over the Overcooked-AI [[35](#bib.bib35)] simulation environment. In these simulations, across five dynamic, partially observable, and high-noise environments, we design and implement a real-time shaping framework that connects proximal policy optimization (PPO)-based agents with frozen LLM evaluations. By leveraging prompt-based symbolic feedback during execution, the framework enables agents to revise decisions mid-episode in response to uncertainty, teammate variability, and timing disruptions. Agents generate structured prompts that encode state, goals, and local history, and use returned judgments to shape the reward signal in a latency-constrained control loop.

We formalize symbolic feedback in multi-agent coordination by adapting game-theoretic principles such as belief revision, strategic consistency, and role alignment into a reinforcement learning-compatible reward-shaping pipeline. This symbolic layer guides agents toward cooperative behaviors by enforcing priors on mutual belief, future intent, and role commitment, without requiring full observability or centralized policy access.

Across five randomized, high-noise environments, including joint observation noise and delayed timing inputs, the results show that the proposed PPO-LLM agents achieved up to a 26% improvement in average episodic return compared to PPO-only baselines. These gains were robust across different seeds and included rare successful completions under adversarial disruptions, where baseline agents consistently failed.

In terms of real-time performance, PPO-LLM agents operated with an average per-action latency of 1.03 to 1.05 milliseconds, inclusive of prompt generation and LLM inference. This satisfies Overcooked-AI’s latency thresholds and confirms the framework’s suitability for deployment in real-time multi-agent infrastructures with frequent decision cycles.

PPO-LLM agents also demonstrated a 35% higher full-task completion rate under noise, reflecting more reliable long-horizon coordination and better adaptation to mid-task disruptions. This includes recovery from failed pickups, bottlenecked transitions, and role misassignments under noisy state transitions.

The proposed approach allowed the agents to achieve a 22.7% reduction in average idle steps across evaluation episodes, indicating smoother temporal coordination, less waiting, and tighter synchronization between role-dependent sub-tasks. This reflects better implicit communication and increased responsiveness to evolving task conditions.

Finally, PPO-LLM agents consistently converged to Nash-like equilibria in cooperative settings such as the Burger Kitchen scenario. Our results in this scenario show that the agents will adopt stable joint policies where deviations became suboptimal. This emergent equilibrium was achieved using symbolic feedback alone, without explicit joint training, parameter sharing, or centralized supervision.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the system architecture, including the real-time shaping pipeline, symbolic feedback loop, and PPO policy integration. Section 3 provides empirical results from Overcooked-AI environments, including performance under noise, task completion rate, latency tradeoffs, and convergence to equilibrium. Section 4 concludes with a summary of findings, limitations, and directions for future research on real-time strategic adaptation using language-based feedback.

## 2 System Architecture

![Refer to caption](2507.02002v1/Model_architecture.jpg)

To support dynamic strategy adaptation in cooperative multi-agent environments, we introduce a real-time reward shaping architecture that integrates PPO with feedback from a frozen LLM. This system is designed to enhance agent coordination through symbolic reasoning and structured evaluations, without modifying the LLM weights or retraining during execution. It consists of six interconnected modules that operate simultaneously during each timestep: i) environment state emitter, ii) observation preprocessor, iii) PPO policy network, iv) prompt generation module, v) frozen LLM evaluator, and vi) reward shaping unit, as shown in Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Dynamic Strategy Adaptation in Multi-Agent Environments with Large Language Models").

At time tt, the environment emits a grid state sts\_{t}, which represents the spatial layout of N=2N=2 agents, interactive objects (such as ingredients and plates), and task-relevant regions (such as delivery counters). Each grid cell encodes the type and state of any entity occupying it. This state is transformed into a one-dimensional observation vector to ensure compatibility with both the PPO policy network and the LLM prompt generator. We instantiate this structure using the Overcooked-AI framework [[35](#bib.bib35)], a cooperative multi-agent simulator in which agents must coordinate to cook and deliver meals under time pressure and spatial constraints. Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Dynamic Strategy Adaptation in Multi-Agent Environments with Large Language Models") illustrates our specific “Burger Kitchen” configuration, where one agent prepares cooked patties while the other assembles and delivers finished burgers. This layout introduces strict temporal dependencies and spatial bottlenecks that require dynamic role allocation and real-time strategic coordination.

The PPO agent, implemented using Stable-Baselines3 [[36](#bib.bib36)], takes the observation and computes an action ata\_{t} based on its learned policy πθ​(at∣st)\pi\_{\theta}(a\_{t}\mid s\_{t}), where θ\theta represents the parameters of the neural network. The policy maps observed features to a discrete set of agent behaviors, such as movement or object interaction.

This action is then executed in the environment, which returns a scalar reward rtr\_{t} and the next state st+1s\_{t+1}. In parallel, a prompt generation module extracts key contextual signals, such as the number of remaining orders and the current timestep, and formats them into a text prompt (e.g., "orders:2 t:25/400").

This textual prompt is evaluated by a frozen large language model (GPT-Neo 1.3B). The LLM produces logits for specific tokens such as "good" and "bad", which reflect the model’s confidence that the agents are cooperating effectively. If the logit for "good" exceeds that for "bad", a scalar bonus λ\lambda is applied:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | λ={λbonus,if logit​("good")>logit​("bad")0,otherwise.\lambda=\begin{cases}\lambda\_{\text{bonus}},&\text{if }\text{logit}(\texttt{"good"})>\text{logit}(\texttt{"bad"})\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} |  | (1) |

If the LLM provides a positive evaluation, the agent’s reward becomes:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | rt′=rt+λ.r^{\prime}\_{t}=r\_{t}+\lambda. |  | (2) |

Otherwise, the original reward rtr\_{t} is retained. The shaping coefficient λ\lambda is manually tuned to remain small and bounded, ensuring stability during PPO training.

The shaped reward rt′r^{\prime}\_{t} is used to compute the advantage function A^t\hat{A}\_{t}, which guides PPO policy updates. We adopt the concept of generalized advantage estimation (GAE) [[36](#bib.bib36)], which links short-term reward shaping with long-horizon credit assignment. The temporal difference error is defined as:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | δt=rt′+γ​V​(st+1)−V⁡(st).\delta\_{t}=r^{\prime}\_{t}+\gamma V(s\_{t+1})-V(s\_{t}). |  | (3) |

Here, γ\gamma is the discount factor, and V⁡(s)V(s) is the learned value function for state ss.

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | A^t=δt+(γ​λ)​δt+1+(γ​λ)2​δt+2+⋯+(γ​λ)T−t+1​δT−1.\hat{A}\_{t}=\delta\_{t}+(\gamma\lambda)\delta\_{t+1}+(\gamma\lambda)^{2}\delta\_{t+2}+\cdots+(\gamma\lambda)^{T-t+1}\delta\_{T-1}. |  | (4) |

Because the LLM remains frozen, its evaluations are deterministic and repeatable. These evaluations instantiate two fundamental game-theoretic principles. The first is belief revision, which parallels Bayesian updating: the LLM adjusts its cooperative judgment in response to evolving prompt content that reflects the current environment state, such as the number of pending orders, role distribution, or elapsed time. This mechanism allows the agent to revise expectations mid-task without retraining. The second principle is strategic consistency, which is implemented by reinforcing only those actions that align with collaborative success. Agents receive positive shaping signals only when their behavior contributes meaningfully to shared objectives, thereby discouraging selfish or unstable strategies and encouraging long-term alignment.

To operationalize these principles, we embed structured symbolic evaluation into the reinforcement learning loop. A prompt generation module continuously encodes task-relevant context, such as pending order count, current timestep, and relative agent positions, which is passed to a frozen LLM that produces a binary cooperative judgment. This symbolic signal is then mapped to a scalar bonus and integrated into each agent’s PPO training pipeline in real time. By providing feedback on the overall quality of collaboration, rather than low-level action success, the framework guides agents toward strategic behaviors that prioritize task flow, anticipation of partner actions, and recovery from errors. This allows for dynamic behavioral adjustments during execution, even in the presence of degraded perception or unpredictable task disruptions. As a result, agents adapt their policies mid-episode using high-level, interpretable feedback. This architecture bridges low-level reinforcement learning with symbolic reasoning, enabling robust coordination, adaptive role assignment, and resilience to uncertainty, including observation noise, partial observability, and real-time variability.

By linking symbolic judgment to policy adaptation, the framework naturally enforces game-theoretic alignment over time. Both PPO agents respond independently to the same symbolic signal and adapt their strategies to maximize cooperative feedback. As training progresses, the agents converge toward a stable configuration in which each agent’s role complements the other. This convergence satisfies the key condition of a Nash equilibrium between two agents: once both agents reach their equilibrium strategies, neither can improve their outcome by deviating unilaterally. Importantly, the framework does not solve for equilibrium analytically. Instead, equilibrium-like behavior emerges through iterative feedback and reward shaping, without any need for direct coordination or access to the co-agent’s internal state.

In summary, we have developed a new real-time shaping framework that integrates symbolic evaluation from frozen LLMs with policy optimization, enabling agents to adapt strategies dynamically in cooperative multi-agent settings. By fusing high-level symbolic reasoning with low-level reinforcement learning, our framework allows agents to revise behavior in real time without the need for retraining, message-passing, or centralized control. This approach offers several key advantages: (1) it provides interpretable, prompt-driven feedback that shapes coordination decisions at each step; (2) it enables agents to handle uncertainty, teammate variability, and perceptual noise through context-aware shaping; and (3) it facilitates convergence to equilibrium strategies via reward modulation rather than direct policy manipulation. The architecture grounds strategic behavior in game-theoretic principles such as belief revision and role alignment, supporting robust adaptation in dynamic environments. These properties make the system broadly applicable to settings where policies must remain flexible, resilient, and efficient under changing cooperative demands. We now evaluate its performance through a series of controlled simulations.

![Refer to caption](2507.02002v1/Overcooked_AI.png)

## 3 Simulation Results and Analysis

We evaluate our framework in the Overcooked-AI simulator[[35](#bib.bib35)], a cooperative multi-agent benchmark in which two agents must complete cooking tasks under time pressure and partial observability. In our custom burger kitchen scenario (Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Dynamic Strategy Adaptation in Multi-Agent Environments with Large Language Models")), Agent A must wait while the patty cooks, then hand it off to Agent B for assembly and delivery. This layout enforces role specialization, timing dependencies, and dynamic coordination challenges that test the ability of our PPO+LLM system to adapt strategies based on real-time symbolic feedback.

As illustrated in Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Dynamic Strategy Adaptation in Multi-Agent Environments with Large Language Models"), the symbolic reward shaping framework is instantiated in this environment, where agents coordinate over spatially separated roles. By linking symbolic judgment to policy adaptation, the framework gradually enforces game-theoretic alignment. Both PPO agents respond independently to the same symbolic signal and adapt their behavior to maximize cooperative feedback. Over time, they converge toward a stable configuration in which each agent’s role complements the other.

This emergent structure satisfies the core property of a Nash equilibrium between two agents: once both adopt equilibrium strategies, neither can improve its outcome by deviating unilaterally. Importantly, the framework does not solve for equilibrium analytically. Instead, this behavior emerges through iterative learning guided by symbolic feedback, without requiring direct coordination or access to the co-agent’s internal state.

![Refer to caption](2507.02002v1/clean_obs_noise.png)
![Refer to caption](2507.02002v1/Bar_graphs.png)

We conduct a systematic evaluation of our PPO+LLM framework using the Overcooked-AI environment to analyze how LLM-guided reward shaping influences multi-agent collaboration, task efficiency, and robustness to uncertainty. Each model is tested over 200 independent episodes per environment, with controlled random seeds and standardized starting conditions to support consistent and fair evaluation.

We evaluate both standard PPO and PPO+LLM agents across four environments of increasing complexity: Clean (no noise), Visibility Noise, Order Timing Noise, and Combined Noise. The metrics include returns per episode, standard deviation, and average per-step latency. We report and analyze results across three core dimensions: performance, robustness, and inference efficiency.

![Refer to caption](2507.02002v1/qualitative_episode.png)

### 3.1 Returns per Episode

![Refer to caption](2507.02002v1/Env_Order_timing.png)

Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 Simulation Results and Analysis ‣ Dynamic Strategy Adaptation in Multi-Agent Environments with Large Language Models") summarizes average returns per episode for PPO and PPO+LLM. In the Clean setting, where agents observe the environment without any disturbance, PPO fails to achieve any reward. This shows that the agent fails to develop cooperative strategies without step-by-step feedback guiding its actions during the episode. However, PPO+LLM consistently has a return of 9.8 with zero variance, demonstrating that binary LLM evaluations are sufficient to support reliable task completion.

Under the Visibility Noise condition, where the agent’s input state is interrupted with a random amount of perceptual noise, PPO again collapses to a return of 0. This outcome shows PPO’s sensitivity to low-level visual disturbances. In contrast, PPO+LLM stays strong and achieves a perfect return of 9.8 again. Since it learns from prompt-driven evaluations that do not rely on precise raw data, PPO+LLM remains stable even when perception is inconsistent.

The shaping mechanism becomes even more impactful under task-level disruption. In the Order Timing Noise setting, where task arrivals are randomly delayed or reordered, PPO performs poorly and has an average return of −40.4-40.4 (standard deviation 3.7). This exposes a lack of stable learning which leads to low-quality actions. PPO+LLM significantly mitigates this degradation, recovering over 10 points (mean: −30.3-30.3, std: 4.4). By consistently evaluating overall task progression (e.g., timestep and pending orders), the LLM provides structure that mitigates the unstable time dynamics that PPO alone fails to handle.

This pattern stays the same in the Combined Noise condition, where both visibility and timing are altered. PPO deteriorates to a mean of −39.9-39.9 (std: 3.6), while PPO+LLM recovers nearly 25% of that loss with a mean return of −29.6-29.6 (std: 4.3). This shows how symbolic feedback helps learning when rewards are weak or inconsistent, by giving the agent a clearer understanding of progress.

![Refer to caption](2507.02002v1/Observation_noise.png)

To illustrate how the system works in practice, we present a qualitative example from the Overcooked-AI environment (Figure [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 3 Simulation Results and Analysis ‣ Dynamic Strategy Adaptation in Multi-Agent Environments with Large Language Models")). In this episode, one agent retrieves ingredients while the other prepares plates and manages deliveries. The frozen LLM rewards states where agents remain active, coordinate handoffs efficiently, and avoid interfering with one another. This leads to smooth, high-throughput cooperation. In contrast, the PPO-only baseline often results in role duplication, hesitation, or spatial conflicts between agents. This example shows that symbolic feedback improves not just numerical performance but also the structure and clarity of collaborative behavior.

![Refer to caption](2507.02002v1/Env_Combined_noise.png)

To evaluate coordination performance under temporal uncertainty, we test both PPO and PPO+LLM agents in the Order Timing Noise environment, where requested ingredients arrive at irregular intervals. This setting introduces misaligned task dependencies, increasing the risk of agents acting prematurely or stalling due to incomplete orders. As shown in Figure [6](#S3.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 3.1 Returns per Episode ‣ 3 Simulation Results and Analysis ‣ Dynamic Strategy Adaptation in Multi-Agent Environments with Large Language Models"), PPO+LLM agents recover from off-cycle prompts (e.g., a tomato requested ahead of time) by dynamically reassigning roles and maintaining structured task flow. In contrast, PPO baseline agents lack a mechanism to reconcile timing inconsistencies, leading to delivery failures and idle outputs. This scenario highlights the effectiveness of prompt-based symbolic guidance in helping agents reason through dynamic task adjustments, enabling more stable coordination even when order streams are perturbed.

To evaluate robustness under perceptual uncertainty, we test agents in the Observation Noise environment, where input states are partially masked or corrupted prior to reaching the policy network. This simulates scenarios in which agents must act with incomplete or degraded visibility. As shown in Figure [7](#S3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 3.1 Returns per Episode ‣ 3 Simulation Results and Analysis ‣ Dynamic Strategy Adaptation in Multi-Agent Environments with Large Language Models"), PPO+LLM agents successfully maintain cooperative behavior, relying on symbolic evaluations that remain stable across noisy visual inputs. The frozen LLM reinforces high-level intent rather than low-level pixel accuracy, enabling agents to avoid collisions, infer teammate roles, and complete deliveries even when specific object placements are obscured. In contrast, PPO baseline agents often misinterpret the scene, leading to duplicated efforts or missed handoffs. This setting highlights the value of prompt-based feedback in providing consistent behavioral signals, especially when raw observations are unreliable.

To evaluate agent performance under simultaneous disturbances, we consider the Combined Noise environment, which introduces both observation corruption and task timing irregularities. This dual-source disruption challenges agents to interpret partially noisy visual inputs while also adjusting to asynchronous order arrivals. As shown in Figure [8](#S3.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 3.1 Returns per Episode ‣ 3 Simulation Results and Analysis ‣ Dynamic Strategy Adaptation in Multi-Agent Environments with Large Language Models"), PPO baseline agents frequently fail in this setting. Visual distortion causes hesitation or miscoordination, and mistimed ingredient requests result in broken task flow, leading to idle or undelivered meals. In contrast, PPO+LLM agents use symbolic feedback to remain adaptive. The LLM reinforces cooperative behavior even under perceptual ambiguity, enabling agents to reassess roles and recover from misalignments. This robustness allows PPO+LLM to maintain productive collaboration despite multiple overlapping sources of uncertainty, demonstrating the effectiveness of language-based shaping in complex, real-time environments.

### 3.2 Robustness to Noise

Figure [4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3 Simulation Results and Analysis ‣ Dynamic Strategy Adaptation in Multi-Agent Environments with Large Language Models") shows the average return per episode under task-level noise. We evaluate each method’s sensitivity to structured disturbances to determine its robustness. To simulate insufficient state visibility, visibility noise modifies the grid-level tensor prior to it reaching the policy network. PPO collapses under noisy conditions due to its dependence on unal tered input encodings for fine-grained value learning, resulting in no reward accumulation. In contrast, PPO+LLM maintains positive returns across both conditions. This demonstrates that symbolic evaluations from the LLM offer resilience by reinforcing cooperative intent, even when perception is corrupted or incomplete.

Since PPO+LLM’s prompt-based evaluation relies on higher-level elements like order count and timestep, which are not directly harmed by visual corruption, it remains unaffected and keeps an average return of 9.8.

Order Timing Noise introduces uncertainty into the environment’s causal structure by changing when new objectives are presented. This disrupts the routine coordination patterns PPO often overfits to. Without the ability to anticipate task sequences, PPO’s policy collapses. PPO+LLM, however, keeps its strategic framework intact by relying on ongoing LLM-guided assessments to judge whether progress is being made. Its behavior remains adaptive, shaped by a reward signal that is context-aware and flexible.

Combined Noise, which is arguably the most difficult condition, introduces both perceptual distortion and goal-timing irregularity, disrupting low-level coordination patterns. PPO’s performance deteriorates substantially in this setting. In contrast, PPO+LLM continues to produce reliably higher returns by leveraging symbolic feedback from LLM prompts. As shown in Figure [4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3 Simulation Results and Analysis ‣ Dynamic Strategy Adaptation in Multi-Agent Environments with Large Language Models"), this feedback serves as an external corrective mechanism, helping agents focus on high-level cooperation rather than brittle stimulus-response loops. This enables more resilient coordination even when the environment becomes unpredictable or misaligned with learned routines.

![Refer to caption](2507.02002v1/Box_plots.png)

### 3.3 Latency Tradeoff

Figure [9](#S3.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ 3.2 Robustness to Noise ‣ 3 Simulation Results and Analysis ‣ Dynamic Strategy Adaptation in Multi-Agent Environments with Large Language Models") summarizes the latency per decision step across four environments. While PPO+LLM delivers improvements in robustness and strategic coordination, it introduces a lightweight runtime cost due to real-time prompt generation and LLM-guided evaluation. In the Clean environment, PPO’s per-step latency averages 0.77 milliseconds, whereas PPO+LLM increases this to 0.99 milliseconds, introducing an approximately 28% overhead caused by token inference and string formatting. Similar latency increases are observed across all settings, but PPO+LLM consistently remains below 1.05 milliseconds per step, ensuring that performance remains within real-time constraints.

Importantly, this overhead is both small and stable. Despite task randomness and structured disturbances, the shaping module’s runtime does not fluctuate due to its reliance on a frozen LLM and a deterministic prompt structure. This predictability is critical for downstream integration in safety-sensitive or latency-bound applications. In addition, because the LLM is queried with compact, template-based prompts, the shaping mechanism remains computationally efficient and scales well across multi-agent deployments. These properties make PPO+LLM viable not just for simulated benchmarks, but also for interactive robotics, collaborative agents, and fast-paced games where decision-time guarantees are essential.

![Refer to caption](2507.02002v1/download.png)

### 3.4 Task Completion Rate

To evaluate whether agents successfully completed the full collaborative task, we introduced a completion-rate metric that counts the percentage of episodes where the total return exceeded a threshold of 9.4. This cutoff was chosen based on empirical observations, where PPO+LLM agents consistently reached scores near 9.8 in successful episodes. Setting the threshold slightly below 9.8 allows for small variations while still representing full task completion.

As shown in Figure [10](#S3.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ 3.3 Latency Tradeoff ‣ 3 Simulation Results and Analysis ‣ Dynamic Strategy Adaptation in Multi-Agent Environments with Large Language Models"), PPO+LLM agents achieved a 100% completion rate in both the clean and observation noise settings, while PPO agents consistently failed to meet the threshold in all environments. In more challenging conditions, such as order timing noise and combined noise, neither policy consistently completed the task, resulting in 0% success. However, PPO+LLM still demonstrated substantially higher average returns in these noisy environments, indicating partial progress toward task completion despite increased difficulty.

These results suggest that LLM-guided agents are more capable of executing full task cycles in favorable or moderately noisy environments and maintain more robust performance under degraded conditions, even when full completion is not achieved. To qualitatively demonstrate this coordination, next we visualize the behavioral progression toward equilibrium in a concrete kitchen setting.

![Refer to caption](2507.02002v1/nash_equilibrium.png)

Figure [11](#S3.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ 3.4 Task Completion Rate ‣ 3 Simulation Results and Analysis ‣ Dynamic Strategy Adaptation in Multi-Agent Environments with Large Language Models") illustrates how PPO+LLM agents converge toward a Nash equilibrium in the Burger Kitchen environment. In Step 1, the agents operate with no coordination, as both attempt to cook or deliver, causing collisions and idle time. In Step 2, one agent begins to approach the burger station while the other still overlaps tasks, leading to partial role confusion. By Step 3, the agents implicitly specialize: one retrieves and cooks patties, while the other handles burger assembly and delivery. Finally, in Step 4, the agents settle into complementary roles that form a stable cooperative policy. Agent A consistently handles cooking, while Agent B manages final assembly and delivery. This strategy consistently achieves high episodic returns (average 9.8 out of 10) and full task completion.

Importantly, this configuration forms a Nash equilibrium because unilateral deviation results in lower total rewards. For example, when Agent A deviates by moving toward the delivery station instead of cooking, both agents experience bottlenecks and blocking, reducing the return to an average of 6.2. Similarly, when Agent B attempts to cook instead of delivering, assembled burgers are delayed or missed entirely, leading to an average reward of 5.9. Since any deviation by one agent reduces the collective outcome and does not benefit the deviating agent individually, both agents have no incentive to alter their strategy once the cooperative equilibrium is reached. This visual progression demonstrates that language-guided agents can internalize equilibrium strategies in dynamic, multi-agent environments and adapt toward optimal joint behavior.

## 4 Conclusion and Future Work

In this paper, we have proposed a framework that integrates frozen large language models with reinforcement learning agents to support real-time strategy shaping in cooperative multi-agent environments. We have introduced symbolic feedback in the form of prompt-based binary evaluations, which refined low-level decision-making without requiring LLM fine-tuning or online optimization. We have evaluated the system across four increasingly noisy Overcooked-AI environments and found that PPO+LLM agents consistently outperformed PPO baselines. In high-noise conditions, we have achieved up to a 26% improvement in average return, while maintaining inference latency below 1.05 milliseconds per decision step. While our framework supports real-time shaping across multiple decision steps, it does not incorporate dialogue-based interactions, such as conversational feedback from the LLM or language-mediated coordination between agents, which may offer richer strategic reasoning and alignment. These forms of interactive feedback and inter-agent communication represent promising directions for future extension, potentially enabling more adaptive and socially aware multi-agent behavior.

Beyond these extensions, several additional research directions remain open. Our current system treats the LLM as a one-shot evaluator. However, enabling iterative and bidirectional interaction between agents and LLMs could enhance strategic grounding and help disambiguate complex decisions. Future frameworks may also incorporate agent-to-agent communication via natural language, supporting joint planning, intent signaling, and belief sharing. While our agents receive symbolic shaping within an episode, they currently do not persist or generalize feedback across episodes. Introducing memory modules or belief tracking could facilitate long-term strategy formation. Finally, although Overcooked-AI serves as a structured benchmark, future research should investigate more complex domains such as competitive negotiation, open-ended roleplay, or real-time robotics. These settings require symbolic reasoning, adaptive coordination, and language-guided shaping, and will further advance the development of autonomous, socially aware, and interpretable multi-agent systems.

This paper proposes a framework for dynamic strategy adaptation in multi-agent environments by integrating frozen large language models (LLMs) with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) reinforcement learning agents. The system introduces real-time reward shaping through symbolic feedback, where a frozen LLM evaluates cooperative behavior via prompt-based binary judgments (e.g., 'good' vs 'bad') and applies a scalar reward bonus to guide agent coordination.

Key technical contributions include:
- A six-module architecture that combines environment state emission, observation preprocessing, PPO policy networks, prompt generation, frozen LLM evaluation, and reward shaping.
- The LLM evaluates high-level contextual signals (e.g., order count, timestep) to produce binary cooperative judgments, without requiring retraining or online optimization.
- The framework operationalizes game-theoretic principles like belief revision and strategic consistency through reward modulation.

Empirical results in the Overcooked-AI simulation environment show:
- Up to 26% improvement in average episodic return over PPO baselines in high-noise environments.
- Average per-action latency of 1.03-1.05 milliseconds (within real-time constraints).
- 35% higher full-task completion rate under noise conditions.
- 22.7% reduction in idle steps, indicating smoother temporal coordination.
- Convergence to Nash-like equilibria in cooperative settings like the Burger Kitchen scenario, achieved through symbolic feedback alone without centralized training.

The framework demonstrates robustness across four environmental conditions: Clean (no noise), Visibility Noise, Order Timing Noise, and Combined Noise. While PPO baselines collapsed under noisy conditions, PPO+LLM maintained performance by relying on prompt-driven evaluations that remain stable despite perceptual corruption.

Limitations acknowledged include the lack of dialogue-based interactions, iterative LLM feedback, inter-agent communication, and cross-episode memory. Future work should explore more complex domains like competitive negotiation, open-ended roleplay, and real-time robotics.

args.key_excerpts: Welcome to Awesome Agent-as-a-Judge! This repository provides a collection of papers for A Survey on Agent-as-a-Judge, where LLM-based agents are used as judges to evaluate different types of outputs, including natural language generation, code generation, mathematical reasoning, and more., The repository is organized into Methodologies (Multi-Agent Collaboration, Planning, Tool Integration, Memory and Personalization, Optimization Paradigms) and Applications (Professional Domains: Education, Finance, Law, Medicine; General Domains: Multimodal and Vision, Conversation and Interaction, Fact-Checking, Math and Code)., Key papers include: Agent-as-a-Judge: Evaluate Agents with Agent (ICML 2025), ChatEval: Towards Better LLM-based Evaluators through Multi-Agent Debate (ICLR 2024), Tool-Augmented Reward Modeling (ICLR 2024 Spotlight), and Learning to Plan & Reason for Evaluation with Thinking-LLM-as-a-Judge (ICML 2025).
args.summary:
This GitHub repository, **Awesome Agent-as-a-Judge**, provides a curated collection of papers accompanying the survey paper "A Survey on Agent-as-a-Judge" (arXiv: 2601.05111). The repository catalogs research where LLM-based agents are used as judges to evaluate various types of outputs, including natural language generation, code generation, and mathematical reasoning.

The repository organizes papers into a taxonomy with two main categories:

**Methodologies:**
- **Multi-Agent Collaboration** (16 papers, 2023-2026): Including CollabEval, HiMATE, ChatEval, and CourtEval, with venues including ACL, ICLR, NeurIPS, EMNLP, and NAACL.
- **Planning** (9 papers, 2024-2026): Including EvalAgent, Learning to Plan & Reason for Evaluation, and Evaluation Agent, with venues including ICML, COLM, DASFAA, and ACL.
- **Tool Integration** (23 papers, 2023-2026): Including Agent-as-a-Judge, Agentic Reward Modeling, VerifiAgent, Tool-Augmented Reward Modeling, and CodeVisionary, with venues including ICML, ICLR, ACL, EMNLP, NeurIPS, and ASE.
- **Memory and Personalization** (8 papers, 2024-2025): Including PersRM-R1, SynthesizeMe!, and GUI-PRA, with venues including ACL, NeurIPS, and ICML.
- **Optimization Paradigms** (8 papers, 2024-2025): Including Incentivizing Agentic Reasoning, Multi-Agent LLM Judge, and SAGEval.

**Applications:**
- **Professional Domains**: Education (5 papers), Finance (4 papers), Law (3 papers), Medicine (5 papers)
- **General Domains**: Multimodal and Vision (4 papers), Conversation and Interaction (5 papers), Fact-Checking (3 papers), Math and Code (11 papers)

The repository has 144 GitHub stars, 7 forks, and is licensed under MIT. The corresponding survey paper authors are Runyang You, Hongru Cai, Caiqi Zhang, Qiancheng Xu, Meng Liu, Tiezheng Yu, Yongqi Li, and Wenjie Li.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
[← All papers](../index.html) [pdf](./2024.EDM-posters.107.pdf) [bib](./2024.EDM-posters.107.bib) [doi](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.12729993) 


FlexEval: a customizable tool for chatbot performance evaluation and dialogue analysis

S. Thomas Christie

Digital Harbor Foundation

Baptiste Moreau-Pernet

Digital Harbor Foundation

Yu Tian

Digital Harbor Foundation

John Whitmer

Federation of American Scientists

# **ABSTRACT**

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed in user-facing applications in educational settings. Deployed applications often augment LLMs with fine-tuning, custom system prompts, and moderation layers to achieve particular goals. However, the behaviors of LLM-powered systems are difficult to guarantee, and most existing evaluations focus instead on the performance of unmodified ‘foundation’ models. Tools for evaluating such deployed systems are currently sparse, inflexible, or difficult to use. In this paper, we introduce an open-source tool called FlexEval. FlexEval extends OpenAI Evals to allow developers to construct customized, comprehensive automated evaluations of both pre-production and live conversational systems. FlexEval runs locally and can be easily modified to meet the needs of application developers. Developers can evaluate new LLM applications by creating function-based or machine-graded metrics and obtaining results for chat completions or entire conversations. To illustrate FlexEval’s utility, we share two use-cases involving content moderation and utterance classification. We built FlexEval to lower the effort required to implement automated testing and evaluation of LLM applications. The code is available on GitHub[1](#fn1x0).

# **Keywords**

LLM evaluation, AI testing, dialogue analysis, open source

# **1. INTRODUCTION**

The use of Large Language Models (LLMs) in educational settings has increased dramatically during the past year with the release of LLM APIs by OpenAI and others. Khan Academy’s Khanmigo is a widely-cited example, but LLM-powered systems have also been deployed to act as tutors [[25](#Xpardos2023learning), [7](#X10260740)], simulated students [[32](#Xxu2023leveraging), [28](#Xschmucker2023ruffle)], teacher coaches [[29](#Xwang2023chatgpt)], essay editors [[1](#Xadewumi2023procot)], item writers [[4](#Xbitew2023distractor), [19](#Xmcnichols2023exploring), [24](#Xosti_10478457)], debate partners [[26](#Xpark2023thinking)], exam graders [[30](#Xxiao2024automation)], and even career coaches [[10](#Xdu2024enhancing)].

Each of these software applications is accompanied by implicit or explicit *design goals*, or behaviors to which the system is expected to adhere. A fundamental design goal common for education applications is that systems avoid hateful, abusive, or derogatory speech, particularly when used with children [[5](#Xcardona2023artificial)]. Another design goal might be that a tutor engages in ‘Socratic-style’ dialogues that guide student through a process of arriving at the correct answer without directly providing a solution [[23](#Xnye2023generative)]. Other goals can be more straightforward to evaluate: developers may prefer short responses, appropriate for WhatsApp-based tutors [[6](#Xchoi2023llms)], or longer responses, appropriate for giving feedback on essay drafts [[20](#XMEYER2024100199)].

Explicit articulation of design goals is necessary for evaluating whether the built system behaves as expected. However, it is not sufficient: the system’s behavior must also be thoroughly evaluated against these goals. In an effort to facilitate automated evaluation of LLM-based systems, we introduce FlexEval, a software system for evaluating the adherence of educational dialogue systems to explicit design goals. To illustrate its functionality, we share example use-cases involving content moderation and utterance classification.

While LLMs are fundamentally ‘inscrutable artifacts’ and can behave unpredictably when prompted with a novel input [[15](#Xkarpathy)], researchers have made progress in standardizing the evaluation of standalone models. For example, HuggingFace maintains a leaderboard in which LLM responses to standardized datasets are quantified and ranked [[14](#Xhuggingface_llm_leaderboard)]. These datasets specify both a prompt and an ‘ideal’ result, typically a short string like a number, word, or multiple-choice response option. Tasks such as question answering [[18](#Xliang2022holistic)], translation [[22](#Xmoghe2024machine)], reasoning [[33](#Xzellers2019hellaswag)], and solving math word problems [[17](#Xlevonian2023retrievalaugmented)] can be formulated in this way. Tools like OpenAI’s open-source Evals[2](#fn2x0) package facilitate the evaluation of foundation LLMs on these tasks.

Evaluation of LLM-based systems, which build upon foundation LLMs to produce open-ended responses, is much more difficult. In educational contexts in particular, the ‘ideal response’ paradigm is a poor fit for generative tasks. A developer creating a tutor-bot has no ‘test set’ of expected responses: there is no ground-truth ideal output. Instead, systems are designed to be conversational and responsive to diverse student input, and to facilitate productive student thought rather than produce specific output. Such systems might be judged on the use of supportive and encouraging language or on giving topical hints phrased in a way a 7th grader would understand. They are also evaluated by what they do *not* say: a tutor generally should not answer math questions for a student, for example, and should never use harmful or inappropriate language, or agree with harmful statements offered by students. System outputs must be reliably accurate and safe for use with students, but manual evaluation processes (including ‘red-teaming’ [[11](#Xfeffer2024redteaming)]) are expensive and slow. Cheaper evaluation enables faster and more confident iteration on product improvements.

Table 1: Configuration options in FlexEval

| **Configurable Items** | **Descriptions** | **Developer Options** |
| LLM completions | Python functions that produce the next dialogue turn based on a conversational history and optionally additional arguments | OpenAI models, locally hosted LLMs, any LLM accessible via API |
| Function metrics | Python functions that evaluate dialogue turns and produce numeric metrics as output | existing metrics in FlexEval (e.g., string length, text difficulty, and harmful content), developer-provided metrics |
| Machine-graded rubrics | rubrics that guide the grader LLM in grading conversational completions or entire conversations to approximate human judgment | existing metrics in FlexEval (e.g., yeasayer effect grading rubrics), developer-provided metrics |
| Grader LLM | LLM models queried by FlexEval to evaluate dialogue turns based on the custom rubrics, producing numeric metrics as output | foundation models (e.g., GPT-4), locally hosted models, deployed LLM applications |

We share FlexEval, an open-source tool built using OpenAI Evals, to facilitate the evaluation of any LLM-based system deployed behind an API. With FlexEval, users can collect ‘test cases’—conversations that led to undesirable system behavior in the past—and re-run those conversations against updated APIs to get new completions for evaluation. Users can also evaluate entire conversations produced by a live model. FlexEval is highly customizable, allowing users to create rubrics and choose an LLM (either a locally-hosted model or an online service) to grade conversations or conversational turns. In addition, users can create and apply custom Python functions to assess various features of LLM outputs (e.g., string length or text readability). FlexEval safeguards sensitive education data by running locally, only calling out to external services for rubric evaluation if requested by the user. Evaluation results are stored in portable formats: JSON and SQLite files. We release FlexEval on GitHub.

# **2. DESIGN AND FUNCTIONALITY**

FlexEval is a wrapper for OpenAI Evals that simplifies the process of creating customized evaluations of LLM-based systems. OpenAI Evals supports the creation and multi-threaded execution of LLM evaluations, including rubric-based ‘model-graded’ evaluations. The Evals tool is extensible, offering mechanisms for adding custom datasets, evaluation types, and integration with non-OpenAI LLMs (generically called ‘completion functions’). However, customizing Evals is non-trivial and requires understanding the structure of the package’s internal classes, configuration files, and folder organization. Moreover, evaluation outputs are saved as JSON and are not easily queryable for analysis.

We developed FlexEval to support the development of LLM-powered math interventions by members of the educational technology community. There is a strong need by practitioners to evaluate the performance of LLM-powered systems in a variety of education-related applications, but OpenAI Evals does not meet these needs as currently implemented. FlexEval increases the ease-of-use of Evals by allowing developers to:

1. define custom metrics as simple Python functions that take text as input and return numbers as output, rather than dealing with Evals’ class inheritance and directory structure
2. define machine-graded rubrics for evaluating conversations or completions, which can be graded by any LLM available via an API call, hosted either locally or on a remote service
3. evaluate new conversation completions (e.g. by a new model version) or historical conversations (e.g. from student interactions with a deployed model)
4. easily test their own applications, as long as they are accessible via a REST API
5. create test suites, where multiple metrics can be calculated against one dataset

The purpose of FlexEval is to reduce the complexity of automated testing, allowing developers to increase visibility into system behavior both prior to and following product releases. To that end, the package provides four files in a single directory that can be edited by users:

* `evals.yaml`: specifications of test suites, including specifications for conversational data, metrics to be collected, the completion function to test (if applicable), and the LLM to use as a rubric grader (if applicable)
* `function_metrics.py`: developer-written Python functions that accept a conversational turn as a string input and return one or more numeric metrics as output
* `rubric_metrics.yaml`: rubrics in the format expected by Evals. These are typically text files with templated entries like `{input}` and `{completion}`, that are automatically filled out and graded via chain-of-thought, producing both a rationale and a score
* `completion_functions.py`: default and developer-  
  written Python functions that accept a conversational history, and optionally additional arguments, and return the system’s next “turn” in a dialogue

Raw data for test cases must be stored in `jsonl` format, formatted as follows and then flattened into a single line per conversation:

```
{     "messages": [         {             "role": "system",             "content": "You are a tutor..."         },         {             "role": "user",             "content": "I need help..."         }     ] } 
```

When an evaluation suite is run, FlexEval constructs the needed configuration files and calls the `oaievalset` command from Evals. Raw results are then saved in a SQLite database. Unlike many services offering LLM system monitoring and visibility, no data leaves the user’s system unless the user explicitly requests calls to an external API for conversation completion or rubric grading.

# **3. EXAMPLE USE-CASES**

To illustrate the functionality provided by FlexEval, we show two example evaluations in some detail. These are not presented as significant findings, but instead as ‘worked examples’ to illustrate the tool’s capabilities. In the first example, we determine whether a pre-release model will agree with harmful statements (i.e., Yeasayer Effect [[27](#Xsarkar2023review)]) or produce harmful statements of their own. In the second, we evaluate historical conversations between a math tutor and students from the NCTE dataset [[8](#Xdemszky2023ncte)] and classify the tutor utterances as either on or off task (an MQI score [[12](#X8b2ecd71-887d-3575-9721-10d7ff508915), [9](#Xdemszky2021measuring)]) using an LLM-graded rubric.

![Given conversation starts, a Completion Function produces new completions that are evaluated by Function Metrics or Machine-graded Rubrics. Both types of outputs are written to an SQLite database.](./flow1_revised.png)

Figure 1: FlexEval’s completion function takes conversational starts and queries a pre-release model to generate new completions. The new completions are then analyzed using a function metric and graded by a grader LLM based on a machine-graded rubric. The results are stored in the local SQLite database.

## **3.1 Testing release candidates for safety**

![A histogram of the 98th percentile of harassment scores orders the models as: TinyLlama, Hermes 7B, Mistral 7B, GPT-4, and GPT-3.5. All models other than TinyLlama have a plurality of A-grade Yeasayer scores, while TinyLlama mostly receives F-grades.](./moderation.png)

Figure 2: Example metrics evaluated via FlexEval. On the left, FlexEval solicited completions from each model to samples from the Bot Adversarial Dialogue dataset, and then scored them using the OpenAI Moderation API. Plotted are the 98th percentile harassment scores from each model, calculated over assistant turns, and higher scores indicate more problematic language. On the right, completions were graded by GPT-4 according to a rubric developed to evaluate whether the completion committed the Yeasayer effect graded on an A-F scale, with F being the most pronounced occurrences of the effect. These 5 models are stand-ins for release candidates and demonstrate the value of increasing visibility into model outputs.

Evaluating model safety is critical when developing applications for use with students because poorly controlled models may produce abusive or unsafe language [[2](#Xbender2021dangers)]. However, assessing whether a certain model or system will produce harmful language is difficult, as the relationship between prompts and responses is often unpredictable. One plausible approach is to collect conversations that have led to undesirable system behavior in the past and evaluate whether the ‘starts’ of those conversations lead to similarly undesirable behavior in updated systems. For convenience in this demonstration, we will perform the analysis using conversations from the Bot Adversarial Dialogue (BAD) dataset [[31](#Xxu2021bot)]. The dataset contains records of humans attempting to solicit explicit or implicit harmful behavior by chatbots.

We processed the BAD dataset to produce conversational starts that led to harmful chatbot productions in the past as judged by human raters. We prompted several LLM models with these starts and collected their completions. We then evaluated the generated completions using both the OpenAI Moderation API and a machine-graded rubric designed to detect the Yeasayer Effect. In practice, developers would replace our stand-in LLM models with the application they are developing. This evaluation can be considered an automated, less expensive version of red-teaming. Results are shown in Figure [2](#example-metrics-evaluated-via-flexeval-on-the-left-flexeval-solicited-completions-from-each-model-to-samples-from-the-bot-adversarial-dialogue-dataset-and-then-scored-them-using-the-openai-moderation-api-plotted-are-the-th-percentile-harassment-scores-from-each-model-calculated-over-assistant-turns-and-higher-scores-indicate-more-problematic-language-on-the-right-completions-were-graded-by-gpt-according-to-a-rubric-developed-to-evaluate-whether-the-completion-committed-the-yeasayer-effect-graded-on-an-af-scale-with-f-being-the-most-pronounced-occurrences-of-the-effect-these-models-are-standins-for-release-candidates-and-demonstrate-the-value-of-increasing-visibility-into-model-outputs). Note that this evaluation is only for illustrative purposes. We recommend users use validated rubrics for this task.

When framed as software testing, each conversational start is a test-case. The system is prompted with each test-case and elicited system behavior is evaluated against success criteria aligned with the system’s design goals. This evaluation comprises a set of functional tests of the software, allowing functionality to be assessed before the system is released to production.

## **3.2 Evaluating completed conversations**

![Flowchart shows Machine-graded rubrics interacting with a Grader LLM. The output of the rubric is written to an SQLite database.](./flow2_revised.png)

Figure 3: FlexEval evaluates entire conversations produced by a live model by using a grader LLM to score/label each conversational turn based on a machine-graded rubric. The scores/labels are saved in a local SQLite database.

 ![F1 scores range between 0.65 and 0.85. Off task, GPT-4 > Mistral 7B > GPT-3.5-turbo. On task, GPT-4 > GPT-3.5-turbo > Mistral 7B.](./on-off-task.png)

Figure 4: Example of custom machine graded rubric to classify teacher turns’ focus on instruction (on vs off instruction task) against human ratings. We used binary classification and report two F1 scores, with either class considered as the positive label. We illustrate the possibility to compare models for grading: GPT-4 and GPT-3.5-Turbo (over API) and Mistral Instruct v2 (locally hosted).

Table 2: Example of student and teacher ‘on task’ turn discourse feature from the NCTE dataset [[8](#Xdemszky2023ncte)].

| **Discourse Feature** | **Example** |
| Student on task | We both have the same number of blue, and red, and yellow |
| Teacher on task | Good, find the range. Find the range. Remember it’s the span of the least to the greatest number. |

It is also important to monitor the behavior of live systems, as they can exhibit behavior not captured by existing test cases. Misbehaving systems can be taken offline or rolled back to previous versions if undesirable behavior is detected. FlexEval supports the evaluation of completed conversations by computing metrics over each conversational turn and then aggregating by both ‘user’ and ‘assistant’ roles.

To demonstrate the analysis of historical conversation, we used FlexEval to score conversational turns from the NCTE dataset [[8](#Xdemszky2023ncte)]. This dataset features classroom transcripts of conversations between students and instructors, along with rich metadata and expert-coded utterance-level evaluations of instruction. We provided FlexEval with instructor utterances and evaluated them by configuring FlexEval to perform a rubric-based evaluation. When run, FlexEval populates user-provided scoring templates with conversational text. The completed rubrics are then scored using chain-of-thought by an LLM grader. To demonstrate FlexEval’s ability to use various graders, we scored the results using both OpenAI’s GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4, as well as a locally hosted 7B version of Mistral. We categorized each instructor turn as ‘on’ or ‘off’ task [[9](#Xdemszky2021measuring)] and compared classifications to expert evaluations. Calculated F1 scores are shown in Figure [4](#example-of-custom-machine-graded-rubric-to-classify-teacher-turns-focus-on-instruction-on-vs-off-instruction-task-against-human-ratings-we-used-binary-classification-and-report-two-f-scores-with-either-class-considered-as-the-positive-label-we-illustrate-the-possibility-to-compare-models-for-grading-gpt-and-gptturbo-over-api-and-mistral-instruct-v-locally-hosted-). In practice, developers could use such post-hoc evaluation to quantify tutor performance or measure conformity to conversational guidelines.

# **4. DISCUSSION & SIGNIFICANCE**

LLM-powered applications have the potential to provide personalized instruction to students at a massive scale. The flexibility of LLMs is accompanied by uncertainty about their behavior when confronted with novel prompts. While this uncertainty cannot be eliminated, it can be reduced. Product developers are increasingly using multiple LLMs or pre-response moderation gates as system components to increase the probability of producing desirable outputs. Even so, the adherence of the application *as a system* to design goals should still be determined.

Automated functional testing of software provides a compelling model for evaluating LLM-powered systems. Application developers create a suite of test-cases that probe the behavior of applications after each new change in the code, with tooling to facilitate the automation process and improve visibility into application behavior. We encourage developers of LLM-powered applications to adopt a similar approach and offer FlexEval to the community in an effort to ease the challenges of system evaluation.

Though FlexEval facilitates evaluation, developers retain responsibility for articulating design goals and creating rubrics that specify whether those design goals are met. LLM-based grading of rubrics is an active area of research (see e.g. [[16](#Xlee2024applying)]). As with human-graded rubrics, LLM-graded rubrics should be validated before they are relied upon in production.

While FlexEval reduces the complexity of LLM-based system evaluation, it still requires tests to be written in a specific format, and requires evaluation functions to be written in code by users. To further increase ease-of-use and encourage widespread application testing, we hope to (1) include a suite of useful built-in metrics, (2) facilitate access to standard testing datasets referenced in the literature (e.g. from [[21](#Xmiller2017parlai)]), (3) provide a user interface for less technical users like teachers or product managers, and (4) create a dashboard for visualization of evaluation metrics.

As LLM-powered products continue to proliferate in education, we believe the excitement surrounding their potential will be tempered by the complexity of ensuring that these products reliably serve students. We share FlexEval as an early contribution to this effort. FlexEval can be easily integrated with other tools, for example by leveraging text analysis functionality from existing tools like NLTK [[3](#Xbird2009natural)] or spaCy [[13](#Xspacy2)]. FlexEval is configurable to user needs, is under active development, and safeguards sensitive educational data.

# **5. ACKNOWLEDGMENTS**

We would like to thank Zachary Levonian for his contributions. This work was supported by the Learning Engineering Virtual Institute (LEVI)[3](#fn3x0) and funded by the Digital Harbor Foundation.

# **6. REFERENCES**

1. T. Adewumi, L. Alkhaled, C. Buck, S. Hernandez, S. Brilioth, M. Kekung, Y. Ragimov, and E. Barney. Procot: Stimulating critical thinking and writing of students through engagement with large language models (llms). *arXiv preprint arXiv:2312.09801*, 2023.
2. E. M. Bender, T. Gebru, A. McMillan-Major, and S. Shmitchell. On the dangers of stochastic parrots: Can language models be too big? In *Proceedings of the 2021 ACM conference on fairness, accountability, and transparency*, pages 610–623, 2021.
3. S. Bird, E. Klein, and E. Loper. *Natural language processing with Python: analyzing text with the natural language toolkit*. " O’Reilly Media, Inc.", 2009.

The flexibility of LLMs is accompanied by uncertainty about their behavior when confronted with novel prompts."; "Automated functional testing of software provides a compelling model for evaluating LLM-powered systems."; "FlexEval safeguards sensitive education data by running locally, only calling out to external services for rubric evaluation if requested by the user."; "Though FlexEval facilitates evaluation, developers retain responsibility for articulating design goals and creating rubrics that specify whether those design goals are met."; "We built FlexEval to lower the effort required to implement automated testing and evaluation of LLM applications."
args.summary:
The paper presents FlexEval, an open-source tool developed by the Digital Harbor Foundation and Federation of American Scientists for evaluating LLM-powered conversational systems, particularly in educational settings. The tool extends OpenAI Evals to allow developers to construct customized automated evaluations of both pre-production and live conversational systems. FlexEval runs locally to safeguard sensitive educational data, supporting the creation of function-based or machine-graded metrics for evaluating chat completions or entire conversations.

Key features include: (1) custom metrics defined as simple Python functions, (2) machine-graded rubrics evaluable by any LLM (local or API-based), (3) evaluation of new or historical conversations, (4) REST API testing, and (5) test suite creation. The tool operates through four editable files: evals.yaml, function_metrics.py, rubric_metrics.yaml, and completion_functions.py.

The paper demonstrates two use cases: (1) testing release candidates for safety by evaluating model responses to the Bot Adversarial Dialogue dataset using moderation APIs and Yeasayer Effect rubrics; (2) evaluating completed conversations from the NCTE dataset by classifying teacher utterances as on/off task using LLM-graded rubrics with GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo, and locally hosted Mistral 7B.

The authors argue that as LLM-powered applications proliferate in education, automated functional testing provides a model for evaluating system behavior. They emphasize that developers retain responsibility for articulating design goals and validating rubrics. Future work includes built-in metrics, standard testing datasets, a user interface for non-technical users, and a visualization dashboard.
