[2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR34 "Hou X, Zhao Y, Liu Y, Yang Z, Wang K, Li L, Luo X, Lo D, Grundy J, Wang H (2024) Large language models for software engineering: A systematic literature review. ACM Trans Softw Eng Methodol 33(8):1–79")).

This review makes the following contributions to the field of agentic AI evaluation:

1.   i.
An evaluation-inadequacy taxonomy mapping 15 benchmarks to deployment failure modes with quantitative gap scoring, distinct from capability taxonomies.

2.   ii.
A critical analysis demonstrating how test-passing metrics fail to capture deployment-critical dimensions (maintainability, security, cost-efficiency).

3.   iii.
A trajectory-level evaluation framework with explicit cost-reproducibility-validity trade-offs.

4.   iv.
A systematic identification of metric insufficiencies including absence of cost-aware and safety-aware scoring.

5.   v.
A synthesis of emerging evaluation paradigms with barriers to adoption.

Software development is a specific field of application of agents on which this paper pays specific attention in the context of evaluating agents. Coding agents are an ideal example of the core problems with agentic behavior evaluation, since they are required to balance between the low-fidel test-passing measurements with comprehensive code quality features such as maintainability, security, efficiency, and compatibility with changing requirements. Although the early analysis of completion benchmarks focused on the single function of a software agent, modern software engineering agents work throughout the entire development life cycle and need evaluation systems to reflect the end-to-end functionality of a software agent, such as requirements analysis, deployment, and maintenance. The conflict between automated measurements and the correctness of humans in software situations sheds light on the general issue of judging agents in all fields.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Sect.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#Sec2) revives historical and technical background agentic AI architectures, core evaluation concepts; Sect.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#Sec7) presents our systematic methodology of selecting and analysing literature; Sect.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#Sec19) surveys major categories of benchmark and evaluation frameworks; Sect.[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#Sec25) analyses evaluation dimensions and metrics; Sect.[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#Sec34) finds applications; Sect.[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#Sec44) explores methodological limitations and open challenges; Sect.[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#Sec54) future directs evaluation applications; and Sect.[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#Sec68) concludes with recommendations on future research directions.

Evolution of AI Evaluation Paradigms and Agent-Centric Benchmarking

## 2 Historical and technical background

This part presents the history of AI evaluation paradigms, starting with the concept of a static task-based evaluation and moving to the agent-based evaluation benchmarking framework, defining the theoretical and technical basis required to comprehend the existing evaluation issues and technological advancements in methods.

### 2.1 Historical background

The development of artificial intelligence evaluation has been followed by four paradigmatic shifts, each of which mirrors the fundamental changes in the nature of AI systems and their connection to the computational environments. Rule-based and symbolic methods predominated the early AI evaluation period (before 2010) with benchmarks concentrating on discrete reasoning problems with deterministic results Du and Ding ([2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR22 "Du W, Ding S (2021) A survey on multi-agent deep reinforcement learning: from the perspective of challenges and applications. Artif Intell Rev 54(5):3215–3238")). The early AI evaluation era (before 2010) was where benchmarks were in the such form of discrete reasoning problems with deterministic answers. The metrics of evaluation were focused on accuracy and precision in closed world assumptions where system logic did not depend on the dynamics of the environment. This paradigm fitted quite well with experts systems and symbolic planners, in which success could be decided by logical correctness.

In 2010-2017, the statistical and deep learning revolution offered large-scale supervised benchmarks that were focused on optimizing single-task performance. ImageNet paradigm created evaluation standards based on fixed datasets, held-out test sets, and scalar evaluation metrics Lebovitz et al. ([2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR45 "Lebovitz S, Levina N, Lifshitz-Assaf H (2021) Is ai ground truth really true? the dangers of training and evaluating ai tools based on experts’ know-what. MIS Q 45(3):1501–1526")). This method was very effective in assimilating perceptual activities and showed underlying constraints in evaluating higher-order cognitive processes, including reasoning and adaptive decision-making Wang et al. ([2024b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR83 "Wang J, Huang Y, Chen C, Liu Z, Wang S, Wang Q (2024) Software testing with large language models: Survey, landscape, and vision. IEEE Trans Software Eng 50(4):911–936")). The benchmarks of this period viewed AI systems as passive functions approximators and quantified what models could predict as opposed to what they could do by sequential action. As systems were unable to cope with distribution shift and task generalization, the difference between the performance in laboratories and in the real-world grew larger and larger Nashaat and Miller ([2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR62 "Nashaat M, Miller J (2024) Towards efficient fine-tuning of language models with organizational data for automated software review. IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering")).

With the advent of foundation models and large language models (2018-2021), the conventional evaluation schemes were broken because they introduced systems that can learn in few shots, instruct, and use crude tools in a rudimentary fashion. The pretraining-finetuning paradigm allowed models to be able to learn generic skills that can be used in a variety of tasks Wang et al. ([2024a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR84 "Wang L, Ma C, Feng X, Zhang Z, Yang H, Zhang J, Chen Z, Tang J, Chen X, Lin Y et al (2024) A survey on large language model based autonomous agents. Front Comp Sci 18(6):186345")). Pretraining-finetuning paradigm enabled models to have general skills which can be used in a wide range of tasks Dong et al. ([2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR21 "Dong Y, Jiang X, Jin Z, Li G (2024) Self-collaboration code generation via chatgpt. ACM Trans Softw Eng Methodol 33(7):1–38")). Initial studies found that Chain-of-thought reasoning and other forms of emergent behavior that were not directly optimised during training were observed in the LLMs, and were not well captured by existing metrics Munikoti et al. ([2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR60 "Munikoti S, Agarwal D, Das L, Halappanavar M, Natarajan B (2023) Challenges and opportunities in deep reinforcement learning with graph neural networks: a comprehensive review of algorithms and applications. IEEE Trans Neural Netw Learn Syst 35(11):15051–15071")). The problem with the use of the static evaluation sets emerged as the evidence was accrued of the contamination of benchmarks by the use of web-scale pretraining data Evtikhiev et al. ([2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR25 "Evtikhiev M, Bogomolov E, Sokolov Y, Bryksin T (2023) Out of the bleu: how should we assess quality of the code generation models? J Syst Softw 203:111741")).

The subsequent emergence of agentic AI (2021-present) has required the very conceptualization of the evaluation approach to be revisited because AI systems have ceased to serve as passive predictors and have become autonomous decision-making agents, functioning in the complex dynamic environments Wang et al. ([2024a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR84 "Wang L, Ma C, Feng X, Zhang Z, Yang H, Zhang J, Chen Z, Tang J, Chen X, Lin Y et al (2024) A survey on large language model based autonomous agents. Front Comp Sci 18(6):186345")). Modern agents have long-term strategic planning, long-lasting memory between agents, can use external tools and APIs, and respond to environmental feedback by adjusting their behavior Nair et al. ([2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR61 "Nair SS, Muddapu VR, Vigneswaran C, Balasubramani PP, Ramanathan DS, Mishra J, Chakravarthy VS (2023) A generalized reinforcement learning based deep neural network agent model for diverse cognitive constructs. Sci Rep 13(1):5928")). This change revealed the deficiency of accuracy-based measures because agent performance lies in the completion of tasks cumulatively, efficiency of resources, and correspondence to human wills in multi-step paths and trajectories, among others, as the human wills are inadequately pronounced in accuracy-based metrics Dakhel et al. ([2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR18 "Dakhel AM, Nikanjam A, Majdinasab V, Khomh F, Desmarais MC (2024) Effective test generation using pre-trained large language models and mutation testing. Inf Softw Technol 171:107468")). Agents were tested in more realistic task environments by specialised benchmarks like AgentBench, WebArena, SWE-bench, MLGym, PaperBench, and BrowserGym, which have been published since the year 2020 and prior to 2020, respectively (Liu et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR52 "Liu X, Yu H, Zhang H, Xu Y, Lei X, Lai H, Gu Y, Ding H, Men K, Yang K, et al (2023) Agentbench: Evaluating llms as agents. arXiv preprint 
                  arXiv:2308.03688
                  
                "); Hou et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR34 "Hou X, Zhao Y, Liu Y, Yang Z, Wang K, Li L, Luo X, Lo D, Grundy J, Wang H (2024) Large language models for software engineering: A systematic literature review. ACM Trans Softw Eng Methodol 33(8):1–79"); Jimenez et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR38 "Jimenez CE, Yang J, Wettig A, Yao S, Pei K, Press O, Narasimhan K (2023) Swe-bench: Can language models resolve real-world github issues? arXiv preprint 
                  arXiv:2310.06770
                  
                ")). Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#Fig2) shows the evolution of AI evaluation paradigms from static task-based benchmarksto interactive agent-centric evaluation frameworks.

### 2.2 Technical background

There are five key capabilities that single out agentic AI systems as distinct and separate as compared to traditional machine learning models. Long-horizon reasoning and planning help agents to break down complex goals into executable sub-goals and have consistent strategies through hundreds of steps of interaction in a coherent way Mohan et al. The evaluated benchmarks (Sect.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#Sec19)) predominantly assess this architecture. While reinforcement learning-based agents (e.g., game-playing AI, robotic control) and hybrid neuro-symbolic systems exist, they employ fundamentally different evaluation paradigms reward optimization and logical reasoning verification, respectively which fall outside our systematic analysis. Our findings regarding metric inadequacy, cost blindness, and trajectory evaluation needs apply specifically to LLM-based agents, though some principles may generalize to other paradigms.

Memory systems include short-term working memory, long-term episodic storage and external knowledge bases that allow agents to have context in real-time, over a prolonged interaction with each other Wang et al. Sci Rep 13(1):5928")).

The methodologies of agent evaluation have key fundamental differences with the classic machine learning assessment on several fundamental dimensions. ### 2.3 Relationship between historical and technical evolution

The historical development of the AI ability and the assessment modes shows certain patterns according to which evaluation systems are always behind the technological one. Fixed benchmarks matched well with the initial AI systems as stateless functions. Terragni et al. ([2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR80 "Terragni V, Vella A, Roop P, Blincoe K (2025) The future of ai-driven software engineering. ACM Trans Softw Eng Methodol 34(5):1–20")). With the acquisition of adaptive behavior by the systems based on machine learning, the evaluation changed towards probabilistic evaluation, although the assumption of passive model operation persisted. This paradigm is disrupted by the shift to agentic AI system and needs evaluation at the environment level as well of courseYan et al. ([2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR90 "Yan Y, Li J, Zaggia C (2025) The analysis of deep reinforcement learning for dynamic graphical games under artificial intelligence. Sci Rep 15(1):23133")).

Greater realism in evaluation brings about harsh trade-offs. Simulated task settings improve ecological validity at great computer cost. The process of benchmark saturation accelerates when competent agents learn to do prevailing tasks, thus requiring the constant creation of benchmarks Lebovitz et al. ([2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR45 "Lebovitz S, Levina N, Lifshitz-Assaf H (2021) Is ai ground truth really true? the dangers of training and evaluating ai tools based on experts’ know-what. MIS Q 45(3):1501–1526")). Agents are prone to increased safety risks when they are put in real-life circumstances with real-life implications. Cross-benchmark comparability is a problem because different structures use different criteria of success and measurement protocols.

### 2.4 Challenges and limitations in historical context

Modern agent analysis continues to struggle with the historical issues of agent analysis. The problem of benchmark overfitting and dataset contamination has been exacerbated by foundation models being trained on web-scale corpora which may contain benchmark data Evtikhiev et al. ([2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR25 "Evtikhiev M, Bogomolov E, Sokolov Y, Bryksin T (2023) Out of the bleu: how should we assess quality of the code generation models? J Syst Softw 203:111741")). The lack of a shared evaluation taxonomies renders formal categorization of agent capabilities and evaluation procedures. Measurement The measurement of generalization and robustness is still unsatisfactory, since benchmarks generally measure how well prediction is on particular task distributions without describing how such prediction will degrade with a change in the distribution of the testNashaat and Miller ([2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR62 "Nashaat M, Miller J (2024) Towards efficient fine-tuning of language models with organizational data for automated software review. IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering")).

The issue of safety and alignment is not given appropriate attention in the agent benchmarks which only ensure that the tasks are done and they do not measure harmful actions avoidance appropriately. Realistic agent evaluation has high computational and financial costs that cause barriers to accessibilityChen et al. ([2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR15 "Chen Y, Xie H, Ma M, Kang Y, Gao X, Shi L, Cao Y, Gao X, Fan H, Wen M, et al (2024) Automatic root cause analysis via large language models for cloud incidents. In: Proceedings of the Nineteenth European Conference on Computer Systems, pp. 674–688")). Environment nondeterminism and lack of proper documentation of evaluation protocols are some of the challenges that face reproducibility. Past tendencies show that the evaluation systems are always lagging behind the development of capabilities. This shortcoming encourages swift creation of ongoing, adaptive, and integrated agent assessment systems that can quantify new abilities and identify safety dangersDakhel et al. ([2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-026-11571-0#ref-CR18 "Dakhel AM, Nikanjam A, Majdinasab V, Khomh F, Desmarais MC (2024) Effective test generation using pre-trained large language models and mutation testing. Inf Softw Technol 171:107468")).

## 3 Systematic review methodology and evaluation techniques

Assessment of agentic AI systems poses methodological challenges never seen before that place it at the core of what is different about the assessment of traditional machine learning. The agentic AI system have sequential decision-making, tool invocation, environmental interaction, and adaptive planning over long periods of time as compared to the static models which give rise to single outputs. It is a systematic analysis of the methods of evaluation that explicitly target agentic systems and presents the methodology as a logical taxonomy that includes the basic benchmarking techniques, interactive assessment procedures, and domain-specific techniques of evaluation. We focus on software development agents (as a main case study), illustrating how the evaluation issues arise in the context of application, and how the issue of architectural decisions has an impact on the strategy of assessment.

### 3.1 Benchmark selection and evaluation protocol

args.summary:
This is an open-access academic article published on April 24, 2026, in Artificial Intelligence Review (Volume 59, article 167), titled "From benchmarks to deployment: a comprehensive review of agentic AI evaluation." It systematically reviews evaluation methodologies for LLM-based agentic AI systems (capable of multi-step planning, tool usage, and environmental interaction). The authors critically analyze 15 major agent benchmarks (AgentBench, WebArena, SWE-bench, PaperBench, MLGym, BrowserGym, HumanEval, MBPP, GAIA, ToolBench, Terminal-Bench, Mind2Web, ALFWorld, BabyAI, and HotPotQA), examining their methodologies, metrics, datasets, and application domains, with software development as the primary case study.

**Key Findings:**
- The paper argues that evaluation methodology (not model capability) is the primary bottleneck limiting reliable agent deployment.
- Quantitatively: 0/15 benchmarks integrate safety or security into scoring; 0/15 include cost-efficiency metrics in their primary evaluation protocol; 13/15 rely exclusively on binary success measures.
- Test-passing metrics systematically ignore code quality, security vulnerabilities, and integration complexity.
- Binary success metrics obscure planning coherence, resource efficiency, and safety violations.

**Contributions of the Review:**
1. An evaluation-inadequacy taxonomy mapping 15 benchmarks to deployment failure modes.
2. Critical analysis showing how test-passing metrics fail to capture deployment-critical dimensions (maintainability, security, cost-efficiency).
3. A trajectory-level evaluation framework with explicit cost-reproducibility-validity trade-offs.
4. Systematic identification of metric insufficiencies (absence of cost-aware and safety-aware scoring).
5. Synthesis of emerging evaluation paradigms with barriers to adoption.

**Historical Context:** The paper traces AI evaluation through four paradigmatic shifts: (1) rule-based/symbolic era (pre-2010), (2) statistical/deep learning era (2010-2017), (3) foundation models era (2018-2021), and (4) agentic AI era (2021-present). Each shift revealed inadequacies in prior evaluation methods.

**Core Argument:** Progress toward trustworthy agentic AI fundamentally depends on evolving evaluation infrastructure beyond binary metrics toward comprehensive, multidimensional assessment frameworks that capture deployment-essential dimensions like cost efficiency, safety compliance, maintainability, and workflow integration.

# LLMs4OL 2024 Overview: The 1st Large Language Models for Ontology Learning Challenge

###### Abstract

This paper outlines the LLMs4OL 2024, the first edition of the Large Language Models for Ontology Learning Challenge. LLMs4OL is a community development initiative collocated with the 23rd International Semantic Web Conference (ISWC) to explore the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) in Ontology Learning (OL), a vital process for enhancing the web with structured knowledge to improve interoperability. By leveraging LLMs, the challenge aims to advance understanding and innovation in OL, aligning with the goals of the Semantic Web to create a more intelligent and user-friendly web. In this paper, we give an overview of the 2024 edition of the LLMs4OL challenge11
1
<https://sites.google.com/view/llms4ol> and summarize the contributions.

###### Keywords:

## 1 Introduction

The Semantic Web aims to enrich the current web with structured knowledge and metadata, enabling enhanced interoperability and understanding across diverse systems. At the core of this endeavor is Ontology Learning (OL), a process that automates the extraction of structured knowledge from unstructured data [[18](#bib.bib18)], essential for constructing dynamic ontologies that underpin the Semantic Web. The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-3 [[7](#bib.bib7)] and GPT-4 [[25](#bib.bib25)] has revolutionized natural language processing (NLP), demonstrating remarkable performance across tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text generation. These models are particularly adept at crystallizing existing textual knowledge from a vast array of sources, making them potentially valuable for OL, where the goal is to extract a shared conceptualization of concepts and relationships from diverse inputs [[13](#bib.bib13)]. The introduction of LLMs has thus opened up new avenues of research, including the exploration of their potential in automating the OL process.

In our prior work published in the ISWC 2023 research track proceedings titled “LLMs4OL: Large Language Models for Ontology Learning” [[4](#bib.bib4)], marked a notable direction towards employing LLMs in OL, demonstrating their potential in automating knowledge acquisition and representation for the Semantic Web. Based on this research, the The 1st Large Language Models for Ontology Learning Challenge at the 23rd ISWC 2024 (1st LLMs4OL Challenge @ ISWC 2024) was introduced as a call for community development. With the LLMs4OL challenge, we aimed to catalyze community-wide engagement in validating and expanding the use of LLMs in OL. This initiative is poised to advance our comprehension of LLMs’ roles within the Semantic Web, encouraging innovation and collaboration in developing scalable and accurate ontology learning methods.

LLMs4OL consists of three OL tasks, Task A – Term Typing, Task B – Taxonomy Discovery, and Task C – Non-Taxonomic Relation Extraction. While participation in all three tasks in the LLMs4OL 2024 challenge is stipulated as desirable, but not mandatory. Thus participants choose to enroll only in Task A or B or C, or Task A and B, or Task A and C, or Task B and C. Furthermore, participants are required to implement LLM-based solutions, we did not impose any restrictions on the LLM prompting methods. For instance, they can choose to bring in additional context information from the World Wide Web to enrich the training and test instances. To thoroughly explore the potential of LLMs for OL, we structured the challenge around two distinct evaluation phases: (1) Few-shot testing phase and (2) Zero-shot testing phase. Through this work, we aim to contribute to the ongoing discourse on the capabilities of LLMs, particularly in the context of OL, and to provide insights into their potential for enhancing the Semantic Web. Thus, in the remainder of this paper, we detail the challenge tasks, what LLMs are being used, participant contributions, and findings.

## 2 LLMs4OL 2024 Tasks

In the LLMs4OL 2024 challenge, we have organized three main tasks which are centered around the ontology primitives [[22](#bib.bib22)] that comprise the following: 1. a set of strings that describe terminological lexical entries LL for conceptual types; 2. a set of conceptual types TT; 3. a taxonomy of types in a hierarchy HTH\_{T}; 4. a set of non-taxonomic relations RR described by their domain and range restrictions arranged in a heterarchy of relations HRH\_{R}; and 5. a set of axioms AA that describe additional constraints on the ontology and make implicit facts explicit.

To address these primitives, the tasks for OL [[23](#bib.bib23)] are: 1) Corpus preparation – collecting source texts for building ontology. 2) Terminology extraction – extracting relevant terms from the texts. 3) Term typing – grouping similar terms into conceptual types. 4) Taxonomy construction – establishing “is-a” hierarchies between types. 5) Relationship extraction – extracting semantic relationships beyond “is-a” between types. 6) Axiom discovery – finding constraints rules for the ontology. These tasks constitute the LLMs4OL task paradigm as depicted in [Figure 1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 LLMs4OL 2024 Tasks ‣ LLMs4OL 2024 Overview: The 1st Large Language Models for Ontology Learning Challenge"). Assuming the corpus preparation step is done by reusing ontologies publicly released in the community, we introduced the following three main tasks for the first edition of the LLMs4OL challenge.

|  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Task | SubTask | Domain | Participants | Phase |
| A | A.1 - WordNet | lexicosemantics | 7 | Few-shot |
| A.2 - GeoNames | geographical locations | 5 |
| A.3 - UMLS - NCI | biomedical | 5 |
| A.3 - UMLS - MEDCIN | 4 |
| A.3 - UMLS - SNOMEDCT\_US | 4 |
| A.4 - GO - Biological Process | biological | 5 |
| A.4 - GO - Cellular Component | 5 |
| A.4 - GO - Molecular Function | 5 |
| A.5 - DBO | general knowledge | 2 | Zero-shot |
| A.6 - FoodOn | food | 2 |
| B | B.1 - GeoNames | geographical locations | 5 | Few-shot |
| B.2 - Schema.org | web content types | 3 |
| B.3 - UMLS | biomedical | 3 |
| B.4 - GO | biological | 1 |
| B.5 - DBO | general knowledge | 2 | Zero-shot |
| B.6 - FoodOn | food | 1 |
| C | C.1 - UMLS | biomedical | 2 | Few-shot |
| C.2 - GO | biological | 0 |
| C.3 - FoodOn | food | 0 | Zero-shot |

### 2.1 Task A – Term Typing

The [Table 1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2 LLMs4OL 2024 Tasks ‣ LLMs4OL 2024 Overview: The 1st Large Language Models for Ontology Learning Challenge") shows 10 subtasks for Task A across 6 distinct domains such as lexicosemantics, geographical locations, biomedical, biological, general knowledge, and food domains. This task is defined as ”discover the generalized type for a given lexical term”. For this task, for each ontology, participants are given training instances defined as following formalism.

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | fp​r​o​m​p​tT​a​s​k​A​(L):=[S​?].([L],[T])f\_{prompt}^{TaskA}(L):=[S?].\;([L],\;[T]) |  |

Where SS is an optional context sentence (if available in the source ontology), LL is the lexical term prompted for, and TT is the conceptual term type. In the test phase, types are hidden, and participants predict them for given terms using their trained models.

### 2.2 Task B – Taxonomy Discovery

After grouping terms under a conceptual type, in Task B, the goal is for given types ”discover the taxonomic hierarchy between types”, where the hierarchy between types is defined with an "is-a" relationship. Participants receive training instances for 6 distinct subtasks (described in [Table 1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2 LLMs4OL 2024 Tasks ‣ LLMs4OL 2024 Overview: The 1st Large Language Models for Ontology Learning Challenge")) as :

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | fp​r​o​m​p​tT​a​s​k​B​(a,b):=(Ta,Tb)f\_{prompt}^{TaskB}(a,b):=(T\_{a},\;T\_{b}) |  |

Where TaT\_{a} is the parent (superclass) of TbT\_{b}, and TbT\_{b} is the child (subclass) of TaT\_{a}. The goal is to train a system to correctly identify the taxonomy between type. The training dataset will include term types and taxonomically related type pairs. In the test phase, participants work with just term types and must use their trained models to identify correct taxonomic relationships (type pairs). The types for the training and test phases are mutually exclusive. Furthermore, for the testing phase participants are required to post-process their outputs to return type pairs that follow the order of superclass-subclass related types.

### 2.3 Task C – Non-Taxonomic Relation Extraction

Nonetheless, the "is-a" relations are not the only relations in ontologies. So, Task C aims to ”identify non-taxonomic, semantic relations between types”. Training instances are given for three subtasks C.1 - UMLS, C.2 - GO, and C.3 - FoodOn as:

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | fp​r​o​m​p​tT​a​s​k​C​(h,r,t):=(Th,r,Tt)f\_{prompt}^{TaskC}(h,r,t):=(T\_{h},r,T\_{t}) |  |

Where, ThT\_{h} and TtT\_{t} are head and tail taxonomic types, respectively, and rr is the non-taxonomic semantic relation between them, chosen from a predefined set RR of semantic relations. Participants aimed to train a system to identify pairs of types, and then classify pairs of types into semantic relations. The training phase involves types, relations, and triples of semantic relations; the test phase requires applying the trained system to predict semantically related triples from given types and the set of relations.

The caveat here is that we do not expect participant systems to infer a semantic relation but rather establish semantically related types and classify their relation from a known set of predetermined relations. This implies that any manual ontology specification task predetermines which semantic relations hold for the given ontology. In an alternative scenario, where participants might have had to infer the semantic relation, we realize that the possibilities of semantic relations might have been rather vast. Hence we posit a more realistic task design by predetermining the possible set of semantic relations.

## 3 Evaluation

There are two main evaluation phases for the challenge, which are the following:

Few-shot testing phase. Each ontology selected for system training will be divided into two parts: one part will be released for the training of the systems and another part will be reserved for the testing of systems in this phase.

Zero-shot testing phase. New ontologies that are unseen during training will be introduced. The objective is to evaluate the generalizability and transferability of the LLMs developed in this challenge.

For evaluation, we used the challenge datasets [[5](#bib.bib5)] -- available at challenge GitHub22
2
<https://github.com/HamedBabaei/LLMs4OL-Challenge-ISWC2024> repository – with standard evaluation metrics used for all tasks. Given 𝒢⁡(i)\mathcal{G}(i) as a set of ground truth labels for sample ii, and 𝒫⁡(i)\mathcal{P}(i) as a set of predicted labels for sample ii, the precision PP, recall RR, and F1-score F​1F1 are being calculated as follows:

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | P=∑i|𝒢⁡(i)∩𝒫⁡(i)|∑i|𝒫⁡(i)|,R=∑i|𝒢⁡(i)∩𝒫⁡(i)|∑i|𝒢⁡(i)|,F​1=2×P×RP+RP=\frac{\sum\_{i}|\mathcal{G}(i)\cap\mathcal{P}(i)|}{\sum\_{i}|\mathcal{P}(i)|}\;,\;\;R=\frac{\sum\_{i}|\mathcal{G}(i)\cap\mathcal{P}(i)|}{\sum\_{i}|\mathcal{G}(i)|}\;,\;\;F1=\frac{2\times P\times R}{P+R} |  |

With precision, we assessed the percentage of the returned related pairs, while recall was used to measure the proportion of correct pairs that were accurately retrieved. In the end, the F1-score was calculated as the harmonic mean of precision and recall, serving as a comparison metric for the participants’ submissions. We used Codalab33

The models are firstly enriched with conceptual information related to terms and types. This is followed by CausalLM manner and task-specific fine-tuning using LLaMA-3-8B [[11](#bib.bib11)]. The proposed approach performs well on several subtasks, showcasing that incorporating domain-specific information and providing a list of classification types enhances inference performance. They concluded that in Task A, GPT-3.5-Turbo [[24](#bib.bib24)] outperformed fine-tuned open-source LLM, and incorporating domain-specific information and providing a list of types at prompt significantly enhances the performance.

The result of fine-tuning on UMLS and GeoNames domains showed that fine-tuning of such model can achieve superior performance. The DaSeLab ranked first place in NCI (0.8249), GeoNames (0.5906), and SNOMEDCT\_US (0.8829) subtasks (scores inside practices are F1-scores).

They showed the viability of soft prompt tuning for OL and the challenge of imbalanced class prompt tuning. Their finding supports the complexity of geographical and biological domains at the term typing task of OL.

silp\_nlp [[19](#bib.bib19)]. The silp\_nlp team participated in all three tasks with a total of 15 subtasks. The results revealed that prompt-based methods were effective in some domains but not universally applicable. Notably, Random Forest models excelled in subtasks A.1 through A.4, while GPT-4o dominated the zero-shot tasks A.5 and A.6, as well as relation extraction tasks B and C. This team obtained in first-place in six subtasks and second place in five subtasks.

TSOTSALearning [[31](#bib.bib31)]. The TSOTSALearning team focused on LLMs such as BERT [[9](#bib.bib9)] and GPT-4. Their findings showed the importance of incorporating rules into LLMs for enhanced accuracy in OL. However, they highlight the challenge of identifying appropriate rules, suggesting that future work should focus on automating rule detection and integrating them seamlessly into LLMs. The WordNet dataset is being considered as a low number of types and having a higher number of types makes it challenging to obtain highly accurate rules.

SKH-NLP [[14](#bib.bib14)]. Team SKH-NLP participated in SubTask B.1 - GeoNames, where they developed a fine-tuning approach using the LLaMA-3-70B and BERT-Large [[10](#bib.bib10)]. Their comprehensive analysis demonstrates that BERT-Large, when fine-tuned, achieves performance close to the larger LLaMA-3-70B model.

Phoenixes [[29](#bib.bib29)]. The Phoenixes team explored the application of a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) approach within the 12 subtaks of the challenge. They introduced a promising RAG-specific formulation over all three tasks of OL, where a RAG system with minor changes was developed for both tasks A and B, later can be used as a two-step approach for task C. Task C consists of the following steps: Step 1 – runs the Task B approach for finding child-parent pairs and step 2 – applying the Task A approach for assigning the relations to the pairs. They incorporated Mistral-7B [[15](#bib.bib15)] as LLM and Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) [[17](#bib.bib17)] model as the retriever model in the RAG framework. However, their results in both zero-shot and few-shot fall shorter than the fine-tuned models and this suggests that still fine-tuning is the key to obtain a high performance within OL.

### 4.2 Large Language Models

The participants in the challenge utilized a diverse array of LLMs, each bringing distinct strengths to the tasks. We detailed a breakdown of the key strengths of the prominent LLMs used.

gpt family – GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4, and GPT-4o: GPT based LLMs, developed by OpenAI, are renowned for their advanced natural language understanding and generation capabilities. These models excel in context comprehension and can handle a variety of queries effectively, making them particularly suitable for tasks that require deep semantic understanding and detailed generation. Their ability to generalize from a wide range of training data allows them to perform well across various knowledge domains relevant ontologies [[4](#bib.bib4), [12](#bib.bib12)]. GPT-3.5-Turbo was a popular choice among participants, with teams such as DaSeLab, RWTH-DBIS, and silp\_nlp using the model and demonstrating its high adaptability and effectiveness across the various challenge subtasks. Furthermore, GPT-4 and GPT-4o as more advanced models over GPT-3, were explored by the teams: TSOTSA Learning and silp\_nlp.

llama family – LLaMA-7B, LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-3-8B, and LLaMA-3-70B: The LLaMA models were another prominent choice among participants. With models like LLaMA-2 and LLaMA-3 featured by TheGhost, RWTH-DBIS, SKH-NLP, and silp\_nlp, their popularity stems from their open-source, efficiency, and scalability. These models’ strengths in handling large-scale data and intricate details made them well-suited for comprehensive multi-dimensional data interpretation.

bloom family – BLOOM-1B7, BLOOM-3B, and BLOOM-7B1: BLOOM [[2](#bib.bib2)] models, featured in our original research work [[4](#bib.bib4)], gained traction due to their open-access nature and collaborative development. TheGhost, in particular, utilized a range of BLOOM models for their flexibility and multilingual capabilities.

biomedical family – BioMistral-7B and OpenBioLLM-8B: BioMistral-7B [[20](#bib.bib20)], as a domain-specific fine-tuned variant of Mistral-7B, and OpenBioLLM-8B [[3](#bib.bib3)], as a domain-specific fine-tuned variant of LLaMA-3-8B, were utilized for their domain-specific strengths in biomedical contexts. TheGhost’s use of these models highlights their importance in tasks requiring detailed biomedical terminology and concepts, emphasizing their significance in the specialized subfields of the challenge.

mistral family – Mistral-7B and Mixtral-8x7B: Mistral-7B, part of the Mistral family of models, was noted for its performance in the challenge by teams like Phoenixes and TheGhost. Moreover, Mixtral-8x7B was utilized by the team silp\_nlp.

others – Flan-T5, GTE-Large, Sentence-BERT, and DPR: Flan-T5 and GTE-Large were chosen for their adaptability and fine-tuning capabilities. DSTI recognized their potential in fine-tuning and handling diverse NLP tasks efficiently when there are limited computational resources. Sentence-BERT was prominently used for tasks involving semantic similarity and sentence-level embeddings. Its popularity among participants like SKH-NLP and Phoenixes. Phoenixes used DPR for the retrieval model of the RAG approach.

### 4.3 Trade-offs Between Precision and Recall

Across the tasks, a clear trend emerges among the participating teams. Teams like silp\_nlp often exhibit high precision but lower recall, particularly in subtasks related to GO and UMLS ontologies. This suggests that while silp\_nlp is adept at avoiding false positives and making accurate predictions, it frequently misses relevant instances, indicating a more conservative approach. However, teams such as RWTH-DBIS and Phoenixes display a different trend, where recall is relatively higher than precision. These teams retrieve a larger number of relevant results but at the cost of precision, indicating that they tend to capture a broad set of possible answers, including many false positives. Their approach may be useful in tasks where coverage is prioritized over accuracy, but it also introduces challenges in filtering out noise.

Teams that manage to balance both precision and recall, such as DaSeLab and SKH-NLP, stand out for their well-rounded performance. These teams perform consistently across different subtasks by finding a middle ground between retrieving enough relevant results and minimizing false positives. DaSeLab, for example, shows balanced performance across multiple subtasks, especially in UMLS-related tasks, suggesting a more effective strategy. Meanwhile, SKH-NLP stands out in the GeoNames taxonomy discovery task, where it achieves high precision and recall, demonstrating its capability to capture relevant information without sacrificing accuracy.

In more challenging tasks, such as non-taxonomic relation extraction, the disparity between precision and recall becomes particularly pronounced. For example, both silp\_nlp and Phoenixes struggle, with silp\_nlp showing low precision but managing to retrieve more relevant results than Phoenixes, which has very low recall. This suggests that these tasks may require more sophisticated models or techniques to achieve higher performance. Overall, the results reflect that teams vary significantly in how they prioritize precision and recall, depending on the specific subtask, with some teams excelling in precision-oriented tasks while others show better results in recall-sensitive subtasks.

## 5 Discussion

Performance Analysis. As the participating teams navigated through the zero-shot and few-shot testing phases of the LLMs4OL 2024 challenge, notable variations in performance underscored the importance of model adaptability and data-specific adjustments. Few-shot tasks, particularly those involving geographical, biological, and biomedical domains, highlighted the critical need for specialized model tuning and the strategic use of training data to achieve high precision and recall rates. This indicates that achieving optimal performance in real-world ontology challenges requires not only selecting the right LLMs but also fine-tuning them to align with the specific characteristics of the domains and tasks at hand. Additionally, studies show that for Task A, even smaller models like Flan-T5-Small with 80M parameters can perform well when there are fewer types. However, as the number of types increases, larger models, such as those with 7B parameters, tend to perform better. One reason for the popularity of 7B models is that Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) [[30](#bib.bib30)] fine-tuning requires less memory compared to traditional fine-tuning methods. Many participants also incorporated external knowledge, such as type definitions, synthesis data using LLMs, or general knowledge graphs (KGs) to build answer sets. These strategies have demonstrated a positive impact on fine-tuning performance.

Complexity Across Domains and Tasks. The results indicated that certain domains and tasks, such as biomedical term typing and non-taxonomic relation extraction, were more challenging than others. The variation in performance across tasks, particularly in relation to term complexity (e.g., Gene Ontology), highlights the complexity of certain knowledge domains. This still requires specialized approaches. The Phoenixes (on all three tasks) and DSTI (on task A only) teams introduced a formulation based on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approaches with success, indicating that combining LLM generation capabilities with retrieval mechanisms can enhance accuracy in OL tasks. This approach is particularly suitable due to the hybrid framework with high adaptability to be extended with different components.

Few-Shot and Zero-Shot Testing Phases. While many models performed well in the few-shot phase, the zero-shot testing phase exposed limitations in the generalization capabilities of LLMs. Models like GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 demonstrated strong performance, but there were notable drops when transitioning from few-shot to zero-shot testing phases. More research is needed to improve the transferability and robustness of LLMs across unseen domains and ontologies.

Task A vs Task C. From a task perspective, Task C attracted only two teams, indicating it was perceived as highly challenging. Non-taxonomic relation extraction requires identifying complex relationships between terms that go beyond hierarchical (taxonomy-based) relations, which is a significantly more intricate task. Unlike simple is-a relationships, non-taxonomic relations are more diverse, context-dependent, and require a deeper understanding of the subject matter. Extracting these relations often involves dealing with ambiguous or implicit connections, requiring models to infer meanings that might not be explicit. This complexity might have discouraged more teams from participating, as success in this task requires advanced techniques, often combining deep semantic understanding with domain-specific knowledge. On the other hand, Task A, term typing, had much higher participation compared to Task C. This task involves classifying terms into predefined categories, a more familiar task for many researchers. Term typing is conceptually simpler because it involves assigning a label to a term, which is something that even general-purpose LLMs can do relatively well. There is a clear, finite set of categories or types, and many participants experimented with text classification approaches.

## 6 Conclusion

The 1st Large Language Models for Ontology Learning Challenge at ISWC 2024 has revealed the emerging potential of LLMs beyond previous studies of OL tasks. The diverse range of participant systems, including fine-tuning, prompt-tuning, and retrieval-augmented generation approaches, demonstrated how adaptable LLMs can be when handling complex ontological data across various domains. The integration of diverse LLMs like GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, LLaMA-3, and Mistral underscored the versatility of LLMs.

Through this challenge, key insights were garnered regarding the strengths and limitations of current LLMs for OL. Notably, while LLMs have shown a remarkable capacity to generalize across unseen tasks (as evidenced by their performance in few-shot and zero-shot scenarios), certain domains such as biomedical and geographical ontologies posed unique challenges, particularly in terms of class imbalance and complex taxonomies. These challenges opened pathways for future research, emphasizing the need for scalable LLM training and the refinement of prompt-based methods to handle highly specialized ontologies.

Moreover, the variety of approaches suggests that hybrid methods combining LLMs with domain-specific knowledge are particularly effective. Moving forward, research should focus on improving the interpretability and scalability of LLM-based OL systems to enable even more accurate and dynamic knowledge extraction. This challenge has laid the groundwork for expanding LLM capabilities in the context of the Semantic Web, fostering innovation and collaboration in building the next generation of intelligent web technologies.

args.summary:
This paper provides an overview of the LLMs4OL 2024 (Large Language Models for Ontology Learning) Challenge, the first edition of this initiative collocated with the 23rd International Semantic Web Conference (ISWC 2024). The challenge aimed to explore the potential of LLMs in Ontology Learning (OL), which is the automated extraction of structured knowledge from unstructured data to enhance the Semantic Web.

The challenge organized three main tasks:
- **Task A – Term Typing**: Classifying lexical terms into conceptual types across 10 subtasks in 6 domains (lexicosemantics, geographical locations, biomedical, biological, general knowledge, and food). Example: WordNet, GeoNames, UMLS, GO, DBO, FoodOn.
- **Task B – Taxonomy Discovery**: Identifying "is-a" hierarchical relationships between types across 6 subtasks.
- **Task C – Non-Taxonomic Relation Extraction**: Identifying semantic relationships beyond "is-a" between types across 3 subtasks.

The challenge had two evaluation phases: Few-shot (using held-out data from trained ontologies) and Zero-shot (using unseen ontologies to test generalizability). Evaluation metrics were precision, recall, and F1-score.

Eight research teams participated: DSTI, DaSeLab, RWTH-DBIS, SKH-NLP, TheGhost, silp_nlp, Phoenixes, and TSOTSALearning. They used diverse approaches including fine-tuning, prompt-tuning, prompt engineering, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). LLMs used included GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4o, LLaMA-3 (8B and 70B), Mistral-7B, Mixtral-8x7B, BLOOM variants, BioMistral-7B, OpenBioLLM-8B, Flan-T5, and BERT variants.

Key findings:
- Task A had the highest participation; Task C attracted only 2 teams due to its complexity.
- Few-shot tasks in geographical, biological, and biomedical domains required specialized tuning.
- Smaller models (e.g., Flan-T5-Small, 80M params) performed well with fewer types; larger models (7B+) were better with more types.
- GPT-3.5-Turbo outperformed fine-tuned open-source LLMs in some tasks; GPT-4/4o dominated zero-shot tasks.
- BERT with rule-based strategies achieved the highest F1 (0.9938) on WordNet.
- RAG approaches showed promise but still fell short of fine-tuned models.
- Biomedical term typing and non-taxonomic relation extraction were the most challenging domains/tasks.
- The zero-shot phase revealed limitations in LLM generalization capabilities.
- Hybrid methods combining LLMs with domain-specific knowledge were particularly effective.

--- SOURCE 1: WebArena Benchmark: Evaluating Web Agents ---
URL: https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/webarena-benchmark

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The WebArena Benchmark is a comprehensive suite for evaluating autonomous web agents on human-like tasks using interactive simulations. It replicates diverse web environments including e-commerce (90,000+ products), social forums (95 subforums, 127,390 posts), collaborative software development (GitLab-like, 300+ repos), and content management systems. The benchmark consists of 812 long-horizon tasks instantiated from 241 templates across all domains.

**Key features:** Multi-tab browser simulation, multiple user profiles, full local hosting via Docker for reproducibility, and functional evaluation based on end-to-end task correctness rather than stepwise trajectories.

**Agent performance:** Initial results showed GPT-4-based agents achieving only 14.41% success rate (vs. 78.24% human baseline). Subsequent advances have raised record single-agent performance to 61.7% (IBM CUGA, Feb 2025). Key improvements came from automatic evaluation with reflexion (29% SOTA gain), self-improvement via synthetic data (31% relative increase), workflow memory and skill abstraction (51% relative boost), structured exploration (Go-Browse), and contextual experience replay (51% improvement to 36.7% on GPT-4o).

**Extended challenge suites:** WebChoreArena adds 532 tedium-focused tasks where top LLMs achieve only 37.8% vs. 54.8% on core WebArena. ST-WebAgentBench extends with safety and policy-compliance metrics, revealing most agents are not yet enterprise-ready.

**Common failure modes:** Prematurely abandoning solvable tasks, hallucinated content, weak generalization, and planning inconsistencies.

**Limitations:** Memory limitations, evaluation precision issues as LLMs approach ceiling, safety and policy alignment gaps, and generalization challenges where task similarity inflates scores without demonstrating true skill acquisition.

**Future directions:** Better differentiation of agent planning/memory/tool use, adoption of tournament-style reference-free evaluation, deeper integration of safety and policy criteria, support for continual learning and modular skill libraries, and ongoing benchmarking of smaller/open models.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: Evaluation and Benchmarking of LLM Agents: A Survey ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2507.21504v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This survey paper, presented at the ACM SIGKDD Conference 2025, provides a comprehensive overview of the emerging field of LLM-based agent evaluation. It introduces a two-dimensional taxonomy organizing evaluation along (1) **Evaluation Objectives** (what to evaluate) and (2) **Evaluation Process** (how to evaluate).

**Evaluation Objectives** includes four categories:
- **Agent Behavior** – outcome-oriented metrics like task completion (Success Rate, Pass@k), output quality (coherence, relevance), latency, and cost.
- **Agent Capabilities** – process-oriented competencies including tool use (invocation accuracy, tool selection accuracy, parameter correctness), planning and reasoning (Node F1, Edge F1, Progress Rate), memory and context retention (factual recall accuracy, consistency scores), and multi-agent collaboration (collaborative efficiency).
- **Reliability** – consistency (pass^k metric for repeated trials) and robustness (performance under input perturbations, error handling).
- **Safety and Alignment** – fairness, harm/toxicity/bias evaluation, and compliance/privacy (adherence to regulations like GDPR, HIPAA).

**Evaluation Process** covers:
- **Interaction Mode** – static/offline vs. dynamic/online evaluation, including Evaluation-driven Development (EDD).
- **Evaluation Data** – diverse benchmarks (e.g., SWE-bench, WebArena, AgentBench, ToolBench, AgentHarm) for domains like coding, web navigation, tool use, and safety.
- **Metrics Computation Methods** – code-based (deterministic), LLM-as-a-Judge (subjective), and human-in-the-loop (gold standard for nuanced tasks).
- **Evaluation Tooling** – frameworks like OpenAI Evals, DeepEval, InspectAI, and platforms like Azure AI Foundry, LangGraph, Amazon Bedrock incorporating evaluation features.
- **Evaluation Contexts** – from sandbox/mocked environments to live deployment.

**Enterprise-specific challenges** highlighted include: role-based access control (RBAC), reliability guarantees (deterministic/repeatable behavior), dynamic and long-horizon interactions, and adherence to domain-specific policies and compliance requirements (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA). The paper identifies future research directions toward holistic, realistic, and scalable evaluation for real-world LLM agent deployment.
</summary>

In contrast, agent evaluation assesses a car’s performance comprehensively, as well as under various driving conditions.", "The evaluation of LLM agents is at the intersection of natural language processing (NLP), human-computer interaction (HCI), and software engineering, which demands additional perspectives.", "Enterprise applications bring additional requirements to agents, including secure access to data and systems, a high degree of reliability for audit and compliance purposes, and more complex interaction patterns.", "Reliability guarantees are especially important in enterprise settings, where agents are expected to operate within compliance and auditing frameworks that require deterministic or repeatable behavior that is explainable."

URL: https://samiranama.com/posts/Evaluating-LLM-based-Agents-Metrics,-Benchmarks,-and-Best-Practices

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage provides a comprehensive guide on evaluating LLM-based agents (both single- and multi-agent systems), covering key metrics, benchmarks, and best practices. 

**Key Evaluation Metrics for LLM Agents:**
1. **Task Success Rate and Stepwise Progress** – Measures task completion fraction and partial progress via milestones or "action advancement" scores.
2. **Tool Utilization Metrics** – Includes selection accuracy (correct tool choice), parameter accuracy (correct API call formatting), and execution success/efficacy (whether tool use improves task performance).
3. **Robustness and Reliability** – Tests performance under paraphrased, noisy, or adversarial inputs.
4. **Safety and Alignment** – Checks for harmful outputs, factuality, guideline adherence, and respectful communication.

**Metrics for Multi-Agent Systems:**
1. **Coordination Efficiency** – Task success per communication (e.g., milestones achieved per message/token).
2. **Communication Quality and Overhead** – LLM-judged scores for message clarity, relevance, and planning coherence (combined into a Coordination Score).
3. **Plan and Reasoning Quality** – Rubric-based scoring of joint plans for completeness, logic, and feasibility.
4. **Alignment and Fairness** – Interactional fairness (respectful tone, transparency) and outcome fairness (equitable task distribution).
5. **Failure Attribution** – Tracing which agent or step caused breakdowns.

**Benchmark Suites Compared:**
- **MultiAgentBench/MARBLE (2025)** – Multi-agent; focuses on cooperative/competitive scenarios with milestone KPIs, communication/planning scores.
- **Self-Evolving Benchmark (2024)** – Single/multi-agent; dynamically generates perturbed test instances to measure robustness via performance drop on evolved variants.
- **Domain Intelligence Benchmark Suite (DIBS) (2024)** – Single-agent enterprise tasks (finance, manufacturing); measures JSON extraction accuracy, function-call correctness, and RAG answer quality.

**Emerging Challenges:** Lack of standardization across benchmarks, scalability/automation needs, difficulty of failure attribution (even state-of-the-art models ~50% accurate), insufficient safety and fairness testing, and lack of cost/efficiency metrics.

**Best Practices:** Define clear success/progress criteria; log tool usage in detail; use layered metrics for multi-agent teams; incorporate robustness testing with data augmentation; include safety/alignment checks; automate evaluation where possible; report both mean metrics and distributions; perform continuous benchmarking; and balance general benchmarks with domain-specific tests.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article (February 6, 2026) by Michael Brenndoerfer provides a comprehensive guide to evaluating AI agents, focusing on metrics, benchmarks, and safety standards. It distinguishes agent evaluation from traditional NLP evaluation by emphasizing that agents operate over extended trajectories, must recover from errors, and carry real-world consequences.

**Task Completion Metrics:** The article covers outcome-based evaluation (binary success vs. partial credit/rubric-based decomposition), success rate (SR) and normalized task success (NTS) formulas, Pass@k and consistency measures (where gaps between Pass@1 and Pass@k indicate reliability issues), and LLM judges for open-ended tasks (noting biases like self-enhancement, length, and position bias). **Trajectory Evaluation:** Process matters as much as outcomes. --- SOURCE 5: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2308.03688v3

SUMMARY:
<summary>
AgentBench is a multi-dimensional benchmark introduced to evaluate Large Language Models (LLMs) as agents across 8 distinct interactive environments, categorized into three types: code-grounded (Operating System, Database, Knowledge Graph), game-grounded (Digital Card Game, Lateral Thinking Puzzles, House Holding), and web-grounded (Web Shopping, Web Browsing). The study evaluates 29 LLMs (including API-based commercial models like GPT-4, Claude, and open-sourced models up to 70B parameters). Key findings include: (1) Top commercial LLMs like GPT-4 demonstrate strong agent capabilities (overall score 4.01), achieving a 78% success rate on House Holding and leading on 6 of 8 tasks. (2) A significant performance gap exists between API-based models (avg. 2.32) and OSS models (avg. 0.51). (3) The most capable OSS model (codellama-34b) scored 0.96, still far behind GPT-3.5-turbo (2.32). (4) Common failure modes include Task Limit Exceeded (weak reasoning/decision-making), Invalid Format (poor instruction following), and Invalid Action. (5) Code training shows ambivalent effects—improving procedural tasks like Web Shopping but harming general thinking in games. (6) High-quality alignment data (e.g., from GPT-4) significantly improves agent performance. The benchmark includes an integrated evaluation toolkit with a decoupled Server-Client architecture, Docker-based environment isolation, and resumable evaluation. Datasets, environments, and toolkit are released at https://github.com/THUDM/AgentBench.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The potential of Large Language Model (LLM) as agents has been widely acknowledged recently. Thus, there is an urgent need to quantitatively evaluate LLMs as agents on challenging tasks in interactive environments., Our extensive test over 29 API-based and open-sourced (OSS) LLMs shows that, while top commercial LLMs present a strong ability of acting as agents in complex environments, there is a significant disparity in performance between them and many OSS competitors that are no larger than 70B., We identify the typical reasons of failures in environments and LLMs, showing that poor long-term reasoning, decision-making, and instruction following abilities are the main obstacles for developing usable LLM agents., Improving instruction following and training on high quality multi-round alignment data could improve agent performance. And different from existing assumptions, training on code present ambivalent impacts on different agent tasks., GPT-4 presents the best performance on 6 out of 8 datasets in AgentBench; on House Holding, it achieves a success rate of 78%, indicating its practical usability in this scenario.

--- SOURCE 6: Multi-Agent Collaboration Mechanisms: A Survey of LLMs ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2501.06322v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a survey paper titled "Multi-Agent Collaboration Mechanisms: A Survey of LLMs" that provides a comprehensive review of collaboration mechanisms in Large Language Model (LLM)-based Multi-Agent Systems (MASs). The paper addresses the shift from isolated AI models to collaborative, multi-agent approaches that enable groups of intelligent agents to coordinate and solve complex tasks collectively.

**Key Contributions:**
1. **Collaborative Aspects & Mechanisms in LLM-based MAS**: Focuses on the operational "know-how" of multi-agent collaboration, including collaboration type, strategy, communication structure, and coordination architecture.
2. **General Framework for MAS**: Presents a comprehensive framework integrating diverse characteristics of MAS, allowing researchers to understand, design, and develop multi-agent collaborative systems.
3. **Review of Real-World Applications**: Examines implementations across domains including 5G/6G networks, Industry 5.0, question answering, software engineering, and social/cultural settings.
4. **Discussion of Open Problems**: Identifies challenges such as collective reasoning, cascading hallucinations, and outlines future research directions toward artificial collective intelligence.

**Collaboration Types:**
- **Cooperation**: Agents align individual objectives with shared collective goals (e.g., MetaGPT, AgentVerse, CAMEL, AutoGen). Advantages include task specialization and efficiency; disadvantages include potential misalignment and cascading failures.
- **Competition**: Agents prioritize individual goals that may conflict (e.g., LLMARENA, LEGO). Drives innovation and robustness but requires mechanisms to ensure constructive outcomes.
- **Coopetition**: Blend of cooperation and competition (e.g., negotiation scenarios, mixture-of-experts). Enables mutual agreements while maintaining competitive elements.
- **Hybrid**: Multiple collaboration channels with different interaction types coordinated together.

**Collaboration Strategies:**

--- SOURCE 8: Evaluating Agent Systems and Human AI Fluency (Part 1) ---
URL: https://trilogyai.substack.com/p/evaluating-agent-systems-and-human

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Evaluating Agent Systems and Human AI Fluency (Part 1)

This article by Leonardo Gonzalez at the Trilogy AI Center of Excellence examines the challenges of evaluating AI agent systems, provides a comprehensive survey of benchmarks from 2023-2025, identifies critical gaps in current evaluation methods, and proposes a **Dual-Layer Evaluation Framework**.

## Key Benchmarks Surveyed

### Single-Agent Benchmarks:
- **OSWorld (NeurIPS 2024)**: Realistic OS tasks; best model achieves 12.2% success vs. 72.4% human performance.
- **GAIA (ICLR 2024)**: 466 real-world questions; humans score 92%, GPT-4+plugins scored 15%.
- **WebArena (NeurIPS 2023)**: 812 long-horizon tasks across 4 mini-web domains.
- **AgentBench (ICLR 2024)**: 8 interactive environments with ~13k multi-turn generations.
- **EmbodiedBench (2025)**: 1,128 tasks evaluating vision-driven embodied agents across 6 capability dimensions.
- Others: SWE-Bench, ToolBench, Mind2Web, τ-bench, TheAgentCompany, ResearchArena.

### Multi-Agent System (MAS) Benchmarks:
- **BattleAgentBench (2024)**: Modified Battle City tank game with 7 sub-stages across 3 difficulty levels.
- **MultiAgentBench/MARBLE (2025)**: 5 scenarios including research co-authoring, Minecraft building, Werewolf, and bargaining.
- **ZSC-Eval (NeurIPS 2024)**: Zero-Shot Coordination benchmark using Overcooked and Google Research Football.
- Others: REALM-Bench, BenchMARL, POGEMA, LLM-Co.

## Critical Gaps Identified

1. **Multi-Agent Coordination Under-Evaluated**: Most benchmarks are single-agent; few assess coordination dynamics, collaboration quality, or emergent behaviors.
2. **Interoperability Gap**: No benchmarks test standard protocols like Google's A2A (Agent-to-Agent) or Anthropic's MCP (Model Context Protocol).
3. **Robustness, Safety & Ethics Insufficiently Tested**: Few benchmarks probe resilience against network errors, UI drift, or adversarial inputs.
4. **Efficiency & Cost Second-Class Metrics**: Compute time, token usage, and monetary costs are rarely reported.
5. **Long-Horizon Planning & Error Recovery Weaknesses**: Agents falter on extended multi-step workflows.
6. **Over-Simplified Environments**: Simulated settings fail to capture real-world unpredictability.
7. **Conflating Capability with Reliability**: Most benchmarks measure what an agent *can* achieve (capability), not whether it performs *consistently* (reliability/pass@k).

## Proposed Dual-Layer Evaluation Framework

**Layer A: Individual Specialist Evaluation** — Tests core competencies of individual agents in isolation (accuracy, consistency, efficiency, robustness, protocol interaction with MCP).

**Layer B: Coordination System Evaluation** — Tests the effectiveness of the entire multi-agent system (task routing, workflow efficiency, communication effectiveness via A2A, global task success, system resilience).

The framework uses a composite score (e.g., 50/50 weighting) with transparent breakdowns for diagnostic insights.

## Recommendations

1. Evolve benchmarks toward realistic, open-ended, robust evaluations.
2. Standardize and deepen MAS evaluation with richer coordination metrics.
3. Incorporate interoperability protocols (A2A, MCP) into benchmark design.
4. Adopt the dual-layer evaluation framework.
5. Prioritize multi-dimensional evaluation including cost (cost-performance Pareto frontiers).
6. Foster transparency and standardization through open-source frameworks.

The article notes that Part 2 will cover Human AI Fluency and the human dimension of agent interaction.
</summary>

However, real-world applications demand reliability: consistent, correct performance (high pass^k)., This dual-layer approach provides granular diagnostics for reliability engineering, distinguishing between failures in individual agent skills/consistency versus failures in system coordination or protocol handling., The over-reliance on static benchmarks that fail to capture these nuances can lead to misleading assessments and brittle systems.
</key_excerpts>

(2025): miscoordination (agents failing to coordinate efficiently), conflict (adversarial relationships), and collusion (agents cooperating against human interests).

The paper recommends: (1) creating more collusion evaluations grounded in real AI threat models, and (2) developing more evaluations based on AI threat models rather than games. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive survey paper on "LLM-as-a-Judge," which refers to using Large Language Models as evaluators for complex tasks. The paper addresses the core question: "How can reliable LLM-as-a-Judge systems be built?" 

**Key Purpose:** LLM-as-a-Judge combines the scalability of automatic metrics with the nuanced reasoning of expert human evaluation, offering a cost-effective and scalable alternative for assessment tasks across domains like academic peer review, model evaluation, data annotation, agent systems, and reasoning enhancement.

**Background & Definition:** The paper defines LLM-as-a-Judge formally as an auto-regressive process where an LLM generates an evaluation (score, choice, label, sentence) based on input data and context. It encompasses roles as graders, evaluators, critics, verifiers, examiners, and reward models.

**Methodology for Implementation (Pipeline):**
1. **In-Context Learning (Prompt Design):** Four evaluation methods: generating scores, solving Yes/No questions, conducting pairwise comparisons, and making multiple-choice selections.
2. **Model Selection:** General LLMs (e.g., GPT-4) or fine-tuned LLMs (e.g., PandaLM, JudgeLM, Auto-J, Prometheus).
3. **Post-processing Methods:** Extracting specific tokens, constrained decoding, normalizing output logits, and selecting sentences.
4. **Evaluation Pipeline:** Four application scenarios: LLM-as-a-Judge for Models, Data, Agents, and Reasoning/Thinking.

**Improvement Strategies (Section 3):**
- **Design Strategy of Evaluation Prompts:** Optimizing LLMs' understanding through few-shot prompting, decomposition of evaluation steps (CoT), and decomposition of evaluation criteria.
- **Model-based improvements** and **Post-processing optimizations** are also discussed.

**Reliability Challenges:** The paper addresses inherent biases (length bias, position bias, concreteness bias) and proposes strategies for enhancing and evaluating reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge systems.

**Applications and Future Directions:** The paper explores practical applications, challenges, and future research directions for improving reliability, scalability, and applicability. It also discusses the synergy between LLM-as-a-Judge and o1-like reasoning enhancement.

The survey includes a quick practice guide for implementing LLM-as-a-Judge systems, covering the stages of thinking, prompt design, model selection, and standardizing evaluation processes.
</summary>

Users preferred GUI for low-level constraints (e.g., JSON output) but natural language for high-level constraints (e.g., tone).

# LLM Agent Evaluation Frameworks

**Updated: 15 January 2026**

LLM Agent Evaluation Frameworks are formal protocols that integrate environment simulation, scenario construction, and quantitative metrics to assess agents' planning, reasoning, and alignment. They deploy modular architectures with agent wrappers, evaluation engines, and aggregation layers to capture multi-dimensional performance in realistic conditions.

## Key Components

**Architecture & Workflow:**
- **Task/Environment Simulator**: Hosts interactive, partially-observable domains (e.g., ALFWorld, WebShop)
- **Agent Wrapper**: Connects LLMs via consistent interface for single/multi-agent pipelines
- **Evaluation Engine**: Records state, outputs, tool calls, memory; calculates metrics (success, sub-goal completion, latency, cost)
- **Aggregation Layer**: Per-trajectory and per-dimension scoring with dashboards
- **Human/Agent-Automated Judging**: LLM-as-judge or multi-agent debate adjudication

**Multi-Agent-as-Judge (MAJ-Eval):** Uses multiple LLM agents with diverse personas to simulate multidimensional human judgment through dimension extraction, persona construction, agent instantiation, and debate protocol. Achieves Spearman's ρ=0.43–0.47 alignment with expert human ratings.

**Dynamic/Adaptive Frameworks:**
- **TestAgent**: Dynamic benchmark construction via retrieval-augmented generation and RL, achieving κ=0.82 human correlation
- **JudgeAgent**: Dynamic interviewer-style assessment with adaptive difficulty control, correction rates up to 13.5%
- **ALI-Agent**: Automated alignment probing via memory-guided emulation

## Metrics & Evaluation

- **Process/Progress Rates**: Stepwise or keyword-based progress rates (AgentBoard, LegalAgentBench)
- **Stepwise/Subtask Metrics**: DAG-of-agent decomposition with interpretable failure probabilities (VeriLA)
- **Tool-Use & Planning**: Component-level tool-match, parameter F1, planning optimality (MCPEval)
- **Safety/Bias/Fairness**: Multi-agent pipelines for psychosocial risk flagging (DialogGuard)

## Cross-Domain Protocols

MCPEval uses Model Context Protocol for portable evaluation across domains. Auto-SLURP and LegalAgentBench demonstrate domain-specific pipelines adaptable to other verticals.

## Open Challenges

1. **Scalability & Cost**: Fine-grained multi-agent evaluation with practical resource requirements
2. **Reliability & Generalization**: Standardizing LLM-judger frameworks to match human experts
3. **Realism & Domain Adaptation**: Covering complex, evolving environments
4. **Automation & Human-in-the-Loop**: Combining automated pipelines with prioritized human oversight
5. **Continuous Evolution**: Maintaining dynamic test suites and adaptive evaluation strategies

The field is transitioning from static, one-shot benchmarks to dynamic, process-sensitive, multi-agent frameworks.
</summary>

MultiAgentBench is a comprehensive benchmark suite for evaluating LLM-based multi-agent systems, published on March 3, 2025, and updated November 27, 2025. It evaluates both cooperative and adversarial multi-agent scenarios, including research collaboration, Minecraft building, database error analysis, coding collaboration, bargaining, and Werewolf social deduction. The benchmark introduces milestone-based Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) that measure not just task completion but also qualitative aspects of agent interaction, including Communication Score, Planning Score, and Coordination Score.

It systematically compares four coordination topologies: Star (centralized), Tree (hierarchical), Chain (sequential), and Graph-Mesh (fully decentralized). Ablation studies show that Graph-Mesh topology yields the best task scores and planning efficiency. The benchmark also evaluates planning strategies, including cognitive self-evolving planning, which improves coordination scores by approximately 3% over vanilla planning to achieve ~4.8/5.

Agents tested include both open-source (Meta-Llama-3.1-8B, Meta-Llama-3.3-70B) and closed-source (gpt-3.5-turbo-0125, gpt-4o-mini) models. Key findings include: gpt-4o-mini achieves the highest average task and coordination scores; coordination score strongly correlates with outcomes; model function-call reliability significantly impacts applied task success; and increasing agent count tends to decrease per-agent contribution but increases total task score up to a saturation point.

The benchmark also observes emergent behaviors like strategic information sharing, trust polarization, and role-driven dynamics. Limitations include reliance on heuristic toolkits for planning evaluation, possible overfitting, and challenges in generalization across open- and closed-source LLMs. All code and datasets are publicly available.

1. **Task Success Rate and Stepwise Progress** – Measures task completion fraction and partial progress via milestones or "action advancement" scores.
2. **Tool Utilization Metrics** – Includes selection accuracy (correct tool choice), parameter accuracy (correct API call formatting), and execution success/efficacy (whether tool use improves task performance).
3. **Robustness and Reliability** – Tests performance under paraphrased, noisy, or adversarial inputs.
4. **Safety and Alignment** – Checks for harmful outputs, factuality, guideline adherence, and respectful communication.

**Metrics for Multi-Agent Systems:**
1. **Coordination Efficiency** – Task success per communication (e.g., milestones achieved per message/token).
2. **Communication Quality and Overhead** – LLM-judged scores for message clarity, relevance, and planning coherence (combined into a Coordination Score).
3. **Plan and Reasoning Quality** – Rubric-based scoring of joint plans for completeness, logic, and feasibility.
4. **Alignment and Fairness** – Interactional fairness (respectful tone, transparency) and outcome fairness (equitable task distribution).
5. **Failure Attribution** – Tracing which agent or step caused breakdowns.

**Benchmark Suites Compared:**
- **MultiAgentBench/MARBLE (2025)** – Multi-agent; focuses on cooperative/competitive scenarios with milestone KPIs, communication/planning scores.
- **Self-Evolving Benchmark (2024)** – Single/multi-agent; dynamically generates perturbed test instances to measure robustness via performance drop on evolved variants.
- **Domain Intelligence Benchmark Suite (DIBS) (2024)** – Single-agent enterprise tasks (finance, manufacturing); measures JSON extraction accuracy, function-call correctness, and RAG answer quality.

**Emerging Challenges:** Lack of standardization across benchmarks, scalability/automation needs, difficulty of failure attribution (even state-of-the-art models ~50% accurate), insufficient safety and fairness testing, and lack of cost/efficiency metrics.

**Best Practices:** Define clear success/progress criteria; log tool usage in detail; use layered metrics for multi-agent teams; incorporate robustness testing with data augmentation; include safety/alignment checks; automate evaluation where possible; report both mean metrics and distributions; perform continuous benchmarking; and balance general benchmarks with domain-specific tests.

# Evaluating Agent Systems and Human AI Fluency (Part 1)

This article by Leonardo Gonzalez at the Trilogy AI Center of Excellence examines the challenges of evaluating AI agent systems, provides a comprehensive survey of benchmarks from 2023-2025, identifies critical gaps in current evaluation methods, and proposes a **Dual-Layer Evaluation Framework**.

## Key Benchmarks Surveyed

### Single-Agent Benchmarks:
- **OSWorld (NeurIPS 2024)**: Realistic OS tasks; best model achieves 12.2% success vs. 72.4% human performance.
- **GAIA (ICLR 2024)**: 466 real-world questions; humans score 92%, GPT-4+plugins scored 15%.
- **WebArena (NeurIPS 2023)**: 812 long-horizon tasks across 4 mini-web domains.
- **AgentBench (ICLR 2024)**: 8 interactive environments with ~13k multi-turn generations.
- **EmbodiedBench (2025)**: 1,128 tasks evaluating vision-driven embodied agents across 6 capability dimensions.
